subtopic: CONTINUANCE OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, is it not going over because the 42 cents a bushel is a prohibitive tax?
The flour that is ground out of that wheat is exported and commands a rebate.
I am glad I got my hon. friends moving; I am glad I have got under their skins just a little.
Oh, oh.

Let me read what they
say about it in the primer which they put out to educate the people on tariff matters. Let me read for their own particular edification:
If the rates are so high, on the other hand, that foreign goods are excluded from the country, a tax is still extorted from the people in the shape of higher prices for everything they use.
Now what answer have you got to make to that? They go further than that. Here is a further extract for my hon. friends to take note of, and you will notice, Mr. Speaker, that they do not refer to manufactured goods. It is the general principle. It does not make any difference whether it is manufactured articles or raw material. Here is the quotation:
As already explained under a system of protection the consumer is compelled to pay a tax upon all imported goods that come under the tariff schedules-
Not on all the goods that come in, but on all goods that come in under the tariff schedules. It goes on:
Upon all goods of domestic origin produced under a protective system the consumer must likewise pay a tax, although in this case the revenue finds its way to the bank account of private individuals alone.
Now what kind of a theory is that to put up?
Is not that right?

Not at all. I ask you now the question: Who pays the tariff tax? But that does not exhaust the points I am going to bring out. I will take now the question of cattle, something that has been disturbing the gentlemen from the west for a long time. They find a difficulty now in selling their cattle. When they want to ship them to the United States, what hinders them? Is it the tax? If the consumer pays the tax, why not ship the goods in and let the consumer pay th; tax?
Does not my hon. friend understand that the tax is so high that the people in the United States will not buy the goods? The tax is prohibitive.
The Budget-Mr. Chaplin

If the rates are so high, on the other hand, that foreign goods are excluded from the country a tax is still extorted from the people in the shape of higher prices for everything they use.
Now let us get along. I, heard in this House a gentleman from the northwest, whose name I do not recall at the moment, describe the situation concerning a carload of butter shipped from some point in Alberta to New York. By the time the freight and duty was paid, he said, there was very little left for the producer. Now what does that mean? Does that mean the consumer in the United States paid that duty on butter, or does it mean the producer paid it? But that does not by any means exhaust the matter. You can take almost any line of goods. I call as my next witness my very good friend the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff), who, everybody will admit, is a perfect free trader, except on the matter of coal. What does he say?
The United States have a duty of from $1.60 to $2 per one hundred pounds on fish.
I ask this question: Do the United States people pay the duty on fish that goes in there from Nova Scotia? According to my friends from the west, they do; the consumer always pays the tax. The hon. member for Lunenburg goes on-Hansard 1923, page 112:
For instance, the business in which I am mostly interested, fish, is hard hit, a duty of $1.60 per hundred pounds having been imposed on salt dry fish, and on salt fish, herring, mackerel and so on, a prohibitive duty of 2 cents a pound. The result is that anybody who ships these goods to the United States receives that much less for them, because the price governing fish is not fixed in the same way as the price on grain or manufactured products, that is, the price of fish is fixed in the foreign market, and consequently the shipper has to pay the duty.
I hope I understand the English language.

The hon. gentleman has been quoting from the Canadian Council of Agriculture, from their platform and the pamphlet written on it. If he reads the English language, he will find a correct answer to his question in that pamphlet.

Mr. Speaker, I think I
know that pamphlet quite as well as the hon. member who has just spoken, and if he will indicate to me where that clause is to be found I will have very great pleasure in reading it. There is not a line in the platform that I do not know; I made it my business to know it; and if the hon. member can indicate to me where that is, I will be very glad to read it.

Who pays the duty on the
Ford cars coming from Detroit into Ontario?

Do not worry, I can
come to that in a minute; but I do not pro-

pose to be taken away from my subject by any outside questions. I invited questions from my hon. friends a minute ago, and I found them pretty mute, pretty timorous, but of course they will do anything to get me away ifrom my point.

The hon. gentleman did
not sit down long enough to allow us to put a question.

I am ready, Mr. Speaker, to sit down at any moment that any hon. gentleman wants to rise. Can it be made any plainer to anyone who wants to listen that this is still another case where the tariff is not always a tax? If so, I would like to know it.
Of course, the same thing can be illustrated in hundreds of cases of manufactured goods. Had I only at the inception taken certain cases of manufactured goods, my hon. friends- as one did a minute ago-would have tried to put me right out of business. I can tell him this. I have been in business forty years. I have grown up in a business from being the office boy to manager. I have during a period of ten or fifteen years occupied the buyer's desk, and I can say that for the period I was buyer, and it was followed up to a few years ago, on everything that was bought and that came in through the customs house the man that sent the goods in paid the full duty. That was part of the buyer's business to see that he got that, and I claim that you cannot have two parties paying the duty. Now as a finish to this-

I suppose that was not
added to the cost?

Mr. Speaker, I did not
see the hon. gentleman rise, although he made some remark.

I would like to rise and ask, if the buyer paid the duty in the first place, was not that added to the cost of the finished article, with overhead and so forth, and the consumer ultimately made to pay the duty?

I did not say that at all.
The hon. gentleman misunderstood what I said. What I said was that the man who sent the goods in here, the seller, had to make a reduction in his price sufficient to pay the duty, and consequently there was no overhead and nothing else except the ordinary profit to be added.	.

If that is the case, then in
what way does the tariff become of benefit to the Canadian manufacturer?

The Budget-Mr. Chaplin

I am relating something
that happened for years under the operation of the tariff. To take care of that very thing the present Finance minister placed a law on the statute book; he enacted a dumping law , to which these gentlemen profess to be so much opposed. That was the reason for the dumping clause. The present Finance minister realized the necessity for it because he sat at the helm and knew what was going on, and consequently he caused a law to be enacted to prevent it from continuing. That is the answer to .my hon. friend. Is there anything more wanted in the way of proof that the consumer does not always pay the duty than the very law enacted by a Liberal Finance minister to prevent the seller from paying the duty?
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to refer to another matter. The Acting Minister of Finance has told us that we have lost a lot of revenue. He has even taken that loss of revenue and put it to good account so as to enable him to say "Why, I have reduced taxation." I want to show as briefly as I can some losses that occurred that were not expected, especially when we entered into the French treaty. I have prepared a list-and I think perhaps this may interest the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe)-of imports from France to Canada and of exports from Canada to France, based upon the ten months of the present fiscal year, 31st March, 1924 to 31st January, 1925, and the comparative figures I will give are for the corresponding ten months periods in each of the years quoted. I give the statement in that form so as to make a fair comparison for the ten-month period in question. The Canadian imports from France are as follows:
1923		 $10,255,000
1924		 13,113.000
1925		 15,167,000
So much for the imports; the gradually ascending scale will be noticed. The Canadian exports to France for the same period were:
1923		 $11,299,000
1924		 15,427,000
1925		 8,383,000
From the sum of $15,000,000 our exports to France dropped to $S,000,000. We started in 1923 with $1,000,000 more exports than imports, and ended in 1925 with nearly $7,000,000 less exports than imports. In other words we sold them this year goods to the value of $8,000,000 and we bought from them goods to the value of $15,000,000. Now I want to point out first of all what these exports consist of. They consist principally
123i
of wheat; pulp; lead; nickel and other ores; asbestos; coal tar; mica; some sugar; canned lobster and salmon; some agricultural implements; and a few scattered articles of manufacture every one of which-I refer to the manufactured articles-will disappear. Why do I say that these manufactured articles will disappear? Simply because the French minimum tariff is too high for us to take advantage of it; we are in exactly the same category in the case of France that my hon. friends from the west are with respect to cattle in the case of the United States. In respect of these exports that we have sold you will notice that in nearly every case they are raw materials: wheat, aluminum, lead, nickel, ores of different kinds; all raw materials. They buy from us a little sugar, a few agricultural implements, and some canned lobster and canned salmon in reduced quantities, because of the fact that the duties have been raised. The articles I have mentioned represent nine-tenths of the total exports and less than $200,000 of our total business was affected by the treaty. In other words, in new business we obtained less than $200,000 and in addition we lost several million dollars of old business. France wants these raw materials and she would take them anj'way; and all we get in the way of new business is less than $250,000. Now, what did we give in return? When we made this treaty with France, Canada gave a list of goods which she could sell to France, and France gave a list of her goods that could be . sold here. France gave us her minimum tariff whatever it might be and she got a fixed rate of duty on a lot of articles. That fixed rate of duty could not be altered by this parliament unless the treaty were abrogated. That is the position in which we are so far as the French treaty is concerned, and we get nothing in return to replace what wo grant. 'When this treaty was being discussed I remember quite distinctly the right hon. leader of the opposition saying to the Minister of Finance, "You should have jacked up your tariff before you went over to France. You should have raised your minimum tariff to a scale that would enable you to trade with them and have something to trade with." I also remember that the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown)-he is not here this afternoon.
He is right here.

Yes, I see the hon. gentleman now. Well, my hon. friend took exception to the statement of the hon. leader of the opposition when he sairi it. would have
The Budget-Mr. Chaplin

been better for the government to have raised the tariff before entering on negotiations, and said that was a principle of questionable soundness. I have no fault to find with my hon. friend's opinion, I think he gave that opinion honestly, but what has occurred? I want to draw the hon. member's attention to this fact. On looking up the British Board of Trade Journal of January 8, I find this statement:
The Board of Trade have received, through the Foreign Office copy of the government bill-
Meaning a government bill in France.
-to modify the French customs tariff duties on some three hundred articles.
And the paper goes on to say:
The explanatory memorandum to the bill, after referring to the general tariff revision now in hand, describes the nature and purpose of the present proposal, which is not intended to replace or delay the normal tariff revision, but is necessary to enable France properly to negotiate the important commercial agreements now under consideration. The bill therefore proposes to increase tariff duties affecting French industries which owing to the burden resulting from the war, cannot face unlimited foreign competition with the present duties.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, what was a matter of questionable soundness for us to do has already been done by France right in our face, and we stand to-day with several hundred articles on which the minimum tariff is to be raised, and what chance have we to do business with them if the minimum tariff is raised, when we cannot do business now under the present tariff? Let me give the House some examples from this, so as to see what it means:
The duty on blankets and camel hair belting is to be increased by over 100 per cent, and wool, etc., astrakans, plushes, sealskins, etc., would pay from 11 to 22 francs per kilog, instead of 8.82 francs per kilog as at present. The duties on elastic and rubbered clothing would be increased by from 50 to 100 per cent; and on felt hats by from 50 to 200 per cent. The duties on the thinner varieties of oilcloth and linoleum would be increased by 25 to 60 per cent, and other waxcloths would also pay heavier duties.
As regards hardware, the proposed duties on locks, keys and nails are some 30 per cent higher than the present duties; those on saws, files and rasps some 200 per cent higher; and those on other tools, needles and certain cutlery about 100 per cent higher.
And so on through the list. There is no use taking up any more of the time of the House with this matter. The principle is there. Canadians as a matter of fact, have to learn to look after themselves, irrespective of the matter of questionable soundness. This may be all right for France, but it is not a good thing for us. This is the first real big joker in the treaty, and there are a lot of them. I am going to detain the House long enough to

give hon. members some more of the jokers in this treaty.
Now, I wish to say a word or two as to the imports. As I said in my opening remarks on this question, the imports have increased from practically ten million dollars in 1923, for the ten months, to fifteen million dollars in these ten months. We have reduced our duty to France on a great many articles so that she could sell to this country. My hon. friends to my left will say, "Oh well, the people got a reduction in the tariff. It makes no difference as long as the people get the reduction in the tariff." On what articles was the tariff reduced? Let me give the House a rough list of them. They are:
Brandy, champagne, wine, silks, satins, velveteens, laces, silk blouses, silk fabrics, silk clothing, gloves, toilet preparations, soaps, perfumery, statutes, china, jewelry, precious stones, ribbons, embroideries, artificial feathers, and flowers, curtains and shams portfolios, purses and pocketbooks.
No doubt, these purses are for the purpose of keeping some of the savings in taxes that the Acting Minister of Finance is giving back to the people. What did we lose? We reduced our duty to many people who could well afford to pay. If you are ever going to get taxes, you have to get them out of the people who can afford to buy luxuries. This is a rich man's treaty-never intended for the poor man at all. Let me give the House a few instances. I will tell hon. members how I figure the duty, because the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) with that even handed way of treating things, will tell you that I have not figured it properly, and if I tell hon. members how I figure it there will be no misunderstanding. First of all, I have taken the duties as they actually are. I prepared the figures actually paid for the ten months on the articles I have mentioned, and I had the customs house of Canada guarantee they are correct. I have contrasted with those figures the duties that would have been collected under the general tariff if we had no treaty. On that basis, we lose on champagne 880,000 in taxes.
From Ontario?

I am not discussing Ontario matters; these are Dominion matters, and for the information of the hon. gentleman who asked the question, I say that we are discussing the budget. We are discussing the budget from the standpoint of the poor people of this country, the people who need to have taxes lifted from their shoulders, and are not discussing those people who are

The Budget-Mr. Chaplin
consuming these goods. The losses are as
follows:
Brandy	 $142,000
Non-sparkling wines	 108,000
Velvets, velveteens and plushes	 65,000
Silk fabrics	 104,000
Ribbons	 31,000
Silk clothing	 44,000
Gloves and mitts	 37,000
Perfumery and toilet preparations	 18,000
Tableware of china	 10,000
Medicinal and Pharmaceutical preparations	 11,000
Castile soap	 7,000
Jewelry	 5,000
What happened further was this:	that
under the terms of this treaty Japan and Switzerland did not hesitate to take advantage of it. France put her goods in at the same rate, and the people lost so much money in taxes, and those taxes that should have come out of the people who could afford to pay them have to be laid on others who probably cannot afford to pay them. I have not the figures for all the articles. If an item did not realize at least $1,000 I did not worry about it; it was not of any moment, so far as my argument was concerned. From France alone, on the goods we imported, we made a loss for the ten months of $991,000; from Switzerland we made a loss of $310,000; from Japan, $232,000; and from Norway $30,000. These figures are for ten months. When these gentlemen went over there to . make this treaty they allowed French nonsparkling wines to come into Canada at fifteen cents a gallon. At the very time they did this the home producer of wine was paying thirty cents excise duty. And they allowed the competitor's goods to come in at fifteen cents. Consequently when the matter was called to their attention they had to adjust it; with this result, that, instead of charging the home producer of wine thirty cents, they had to reduce the tax to seven and a half cents in order to place the home producer on an equality. I say that anybody at home who can afford to buy an article like wine can afford to pay a tax, and the tax of thirty cents was reasonable and just. But owing to the treaty this tax had to be reduced, and we lost on that operation on that article the sum of $129,000. The total loss was $1,695,000 for the ten months which I have mentioned. If you add two months more on the same basis, it means a loss in revenue of over two million dollars.
Besides the one big joker in this treaty to which I have referred, there are some others. I have not time to refer to half of them here, but I will give the House a few just for the edification of hon. members. Take the item
of gloves and mitts. We reduced our tariff and France gave us her new tariff on gloves and mitts to France to the minimum tariff, but the minimum tariff is so high that we did not ship any, while France shipped us $383,000 worth. We lost in duty over what we had sold to them before, $37,000.
As regards tableware of china, we reduced our duty to France, and France very accommodatingly reduced her duty to us. Just imagine reducing the duty for us to ship tableware of china into France 1 The result was that France sold us all the china, we did not sell her any; and we lost in revenue $11,000. The poor working man in this country saved $11,000 on his china. As regards perfumery and toilet preparations, we lost in revenue $18,000. We gave France fixed rates of duty and we could not change the duty to-morrow if we wanted to do so.
Let me give the House an idea of what comes into this country in the way of nonsparkling wines. In ten months of 1923 there were imported 56,000 gallons and, in 1924-5,
134,000	gallons. We lost in revenue on this item over $100,000. This is supposed to be a temperance country. The hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) asked:	Was it in Ontario where this wine
was used? Before he goes out I should like to give him the figures in regard to the item of brandy. I do not think it was in Ontario, but I will give him the result. In 1923 we imported 43,000 gallons, and in ten months of
1924-5 we imported 146,000 gallons. That is pretty good for a temperance country. Our loss in revenue on that item alone was $142,000.
Let us take the item of canned fruits and canned vegetables on which we gave France fixed rates of duties. We had a loss of revenue. We sold no fruits but we sold them $800 worth of canned vegetables. Just imagine 1 We sold France $800 worth of canned vegetables! In 1920, we sold France $1,000,000 of canned fruits and in 1924-5 we sold nothing. Why? Simply because the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries, the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) went to France and made a treaty with her by [DOT] which France had fixed rates of duties on importations into Canada of canned fruits, and the duties that we have to pay on our importations into France are higher than those she has to pay on importations into Canada. That is another joker in the treaty.
On cutlery and jewellery we lost in revenue $8,000. The Minister of Justice in his address last year told us th?' was going to sell
The Budget- Mr. Chaplin

butter to France. He reduced the duty on fresh butter so that our butter would get in. This is what he said:
We have not negotiated a treaty for the Pilgrim Fathers or for the farmers that came with Cartier or Champlain, we have negotiated a treaty for the farmers of the present.
Let me tell the Minister of Justice that the Pilgrim Fathers and the farmers that came with Cartier or Champlain shipped as much butter to France last year, as the present fanners did. Dead as they are, they shipped not a pound, and neither did the living farmers.
A few years ago we shipped condensed milk to France. In 1922, for instance, we shipped $568,000 worth. The duty was increased by fifty per cent, and last year we sold France
87,000	worth. That is another joker. The Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) whom I saw here a minute ago, made a prediction in 1923. He said:
Canada will export boots and shoes to France.
I have looked up the records and I find that no leather boots and shoes went to France, although a few rubbers went. I suppose -we shall have another shot about bronze powder from him too. Last year the story was: "Oh, well, we did not make the records." A lot of bronze powder was exported from this country. The minister produced a telegram from a manufacturer stating that they exported a lot of bronze powder. When I said to the minister:	"This does not appear in the export
records," he said:	"We did not prepare those
records; you prepared them." I have examined the records for the last four years and there are no exports of bronze powder. The minister should communicate with the manufacturers and find out where this stuff 'has gone. It must have gone somewhere and we cannot find it.
Let me mention a few other articles that we used to send to France. In 1920, we shipped $275,000 worth of dried apples; now this trade is gone. In 1922, we sold France $455,000 worth of oats; in 1925, there is no trade-nothing doing.
I cannot pass over this list of luxuries without reading an extract from a speech made by the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond). We .all know that very delightful gentleman. We all have heard from him of the distress that exists in Brantford, and now that we look back on the matter, we come to the conclusion that the people of Brantford have not gone away because of lack of work. I will let hon. members conclude what the reason is when I read his speech. He said:

In the part of the country that I came from, I beg to say that brandy and champagne are not luxuries, nor, Sir, is sparkling burgundy any luxury. On the contrary, these things are classed with blue pills, calomel and salts.
We had heard that its industries were languishing and its population was scattered, but we are glad to know that its necessities are well looked after. I am afraid that these gentlemen who are out of work in Brantford, instead of having gone away to other localities to look for work, have gone to California or to Florida, and may come back, who knows, in their luxurious motor cars, wearing the luxuries of which I have spoken . I rcgr t having taken up so much of the time of the House and I hope I have not tired hon. members too much.
What about that long list of drugs which appears :n the treaty? Did we sell any of them?

Answering the question
of the leader of the opposition, I beg ,to say that of all those padded sheets of drugs, several pages, ccntaining some 150 articles, I think there is one on the list of exports, and others that we exported before, now disappear from the list.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget is one
of the time-honoured institutions of this parliament. It affords an opportunity, not only of discussing the financial affairs of the country for and against the ministry s view of these matters, but further of ventilating grievances and especially of discussing problems which members would not get as good an opportunity of discussing later on in the session. I have to congratulate the official opposition upon their mathematical attainments while discussing this particular budget. They started off with a surplus of nearly two millions and by the time this had passed through various hands it had mounted considerably. First, some hon. gentlemen added gently to it making it five or six millions and then later on it was augmented very materially. I cannot recall just now the particular gentlemen wh* added to it but I remember that the hon member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) and the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) as well as the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) all had a hand in it. All these hon. gentlemen gave it the once-over, so to speak, and each time they made it a little more imposing until finally, when the hon. and genial member for Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie) had got through with it, it assumed the formidable proportions of 8100,000,000.

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
That statement was made in the very first speech in the debate from this side of the House.

I did not know
that, but at all events some hon. gentlemen evidently receded from that bold position at first although ultimately they took it up again. And I am afraid that had it not been for the approach of the Easter season, which sometimes has a disciplinary effect on mortals, that S100,000,000 would before long have increased to several hundred millions. Heaven only knows now what it may be after Easter.
I shall now refer to some of the remarks made'by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre and the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy Raver. Exception has been taken by these gentlemen to what they call extravagance on the part of the government, but it will be noted that very few individual items are cited; we have nothing but generalities. The government is brought under one wholesale charge of extravagance and it is said that so bad is this evil that taxation is mounting skyward. And how do hon. gentlemen opposite propose to bring down this mounting taxation? Why, they want to have more protection ; high taxation is to be cured by higher taxation. And so these gentlemen go on proposing their nostrums indefinitely. But the only particular item to which the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River objected, so far as I could notice, was the alleged extravagance in connection with commissions of investigation, one or two of which he mentioned. The hon. member referred for example to the grain inquiry. Now what is the history of that? It is merely a continuation of an inquiry that was started by the preceding government of which the hon. gentleman himself was for a short time a member. That investigating body created at that time perambulated the whole country, 5 p.m. creating a good deal of consternation because of their crude methods; and things had reached such a pitch that an injunction was sought against their further inquiries. And between these injunctions and their waiting and hovering around, and the fact that the whole country at that time was upset over the prospects of an election, coupled with the further fact that their revenues had been exhausted, they simply hung on until by December 6 they and the government went out together. We had to do something in the matter; and, as will be recalled, the next year the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) voiced the opinion that the inquiiy should be resumed; that was what he urged. So that we find one wing of
the opposition, the official section, the year before starting an inquiry but achieving nothing, not even a report being presented, followed b3- another wing of the opposition, the unofficial section, recommending later to this government, through a resolution offered by one of its members and accepted) that the government take up the matter again and proceed with the investigation. And that has been done. Well, where is the extravagance in that? Have we not got value thus far? We have a report upon the subject and a bill will be introduced after the Easter holidays. But there was absolutely nothing to show as a result of the first inquiry started by the government of which the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River was a member for a very short time. If this is the only extravagance to which hon. gentlemen can point it is surely a very minor one. But it has not been proved that even here there has been any extravagance, because after all, in view of the importance of the subject, the expenditure that has been involved is very small.

I want to object to one
expression the hon. member has used which I will not let pass: he referred to us in this part of the chamber as the "unofficial opposition." We are not an opposition.

I do not know what the proper term should be. Hon. gentlemen say they are not a party and now the hon. gentleman says they are not an unofficial opposition. I suppose they are just neutral; maybe that word would do.
Probably that would do.

Yes, a neutrai
party ready to condone or condemn as the circumstances warrant.
Complete the sentence.
That is the complete sentence-a neutral party ready to condone or condemn as the circumstances warrant.
Or to praise if necessary.
Well, condone would be equivalent to that.
Oh, oh.

W'e will accept
that word praise too; I aim ready to add that to the qualification. Now, to proceed. That was the extent of the extravagance with which the government was charged by the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River. It will be remembered also that when the estimates of the Minister of Public

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
Works (Mr. King, Kootenay) were going through the House the hon. member for Vancouver Centre at one stage discussed the question of over-manning in the civil service, denouncing all and sundry. I do not think he said that the civil servants were paid too much but he did say that there were too many civil servants; he gave us that old chestnut-too much overlapping in the civil service. Well, I would take it as a friendly act on the part of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre or of any other hon. gentleman in this House if he would be good enough to point out where, among the 1,200 cavil servants in the Department of Agriculture, the services of any one could be dispensed with without sacrificing in some measure the interests of the public service. If the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie) were in his place I would ask him, as one who is familiar with the work of the department, to point out where I could dispense with one man without some sacrifice. On the contrary, I know where I could engage a good many more men profitably. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre has himself pointed out on several occasions the disabilities arising in his constituency in connection with the shipment of certain goods packed in straw; and ultimately I believe we shall have to appoint a few more men at that point to take care of that situation. We do not want to do this if it is at all avoidable, but this is one answer to the charge of overlapping in the service. And this same thing is true all along the line; in a dozen directions, instead of there being too many public servants there are too few, to the detriment of the public interest. But the public do not think that; they hear a clamour from one side of the chamber to the other declaiming against the multitude of civil servants, all this talk often reflecting unwarrantably on the ability of these people. I leave the invitation open to any hon. gentleman in the House to show where any services can be dispensed with or economies effected in the votes presented to the House for the department. I speak more particularly for my own department because I am more familiar with it; but there is no member of 'this government who is not ready to give the same invitation and who would not be met with the same silence. So much for that. There are more remarks in this connection but I shall reserve them for more convenient seasons.
The hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River did take up the other day a question that required some explanation. He

gave a part of the information practically correct, and that was as to the imports of a large number of agricultural commodities, which he said should have been grown in Canada; and for some reason or other he suggested that someone was to blame, the government presumably. I shall refer to the list, and I shall mention not only imports but exports as well, for unless you have the two you will not understand the situation in regard to the imports. I shall interject an explanation here and there as I go along. In the year ending March 31, 1924, we imported of butter, in round figures, 1,500,000 pounds and exported 13,000,000 pounds. This year we exported 20,000,000 pounds; the importations are decreasing while the exports are increasing. Of cheese we imported 1,500,000 pounds and exported 116,000,000 pounds. This is nearly all fancy cheese, made in Italy, Switzerland, and elsewhere, which we do not produce in Canada.
Of eggs, the number of dozens imported was 6.500,000 in round numbers, while the export was 2,890.000. This situation is improving yearly. The year before, the imports were 8,000.000 and the exports some
3,000,000. In addition to that, owing to the improved quality of our eggs the consumption in Canada has increased during the last four or five years from sixteen dozen per annum per capita to twenty-six dozen per capita, an increase of about 60 per cent. That is because the eggs are better. So that the exports and imports of this commodity do not at all show the production.
Is the grading of eggs in country districts under the minister's department?
Yes.
The provincial governments have nothing to do with it?

No, not now; they did a few years ago. There were a number of provincial methods of dealing with it, starting I think with Prince Edward Island about twelve years ago and then being taken up by the western provinces. On account of the expert character of the work it was thought wise to make it uniform and have the whole thing come under the federal Department of Agriculture. At another time when this matter is up I will perhaps make a fuller explanation.
Of fruits, $18,000,000 worth were imported in the year to which I refer, and nearly $9,000,000 worth were exported. Fruits are a very healthful commodity. A great many

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
of them come in free and are available at times when our own fruit is not available. But it will be noted that to offset the large amount of imports we have nearly $9,000,000 of exports.
The question of hides has been the subject of much discussion. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) and one or two other Progressives drew attention to the comparatively small price of our hides and the large import. In the particular year to which I refer 46,000,000 pounds of hides were imported, chiefly from the United States, Argentine and New Zealand, and against that,
49,000,000 pounds were exported. Apparently the users of hides, the boot and shoe makers, buy foreign hides because of the greater uniformity in the article; it suits their trade better. Every farmer in this chamber is familiar with the irregularity of the quality of a great many of the country-killed hides, especially in the winter. I do not know whether that is the reason why these are exported; I suppose it is because it is to the advantage of the sellers to export them and that the quality of the product is perhaps more suitable to the export trade.
On the question of hides, has the minister gone into the imports or exports of tanned leather made from these hides that are imported?
No.
It would be found very interesting.

I took just the list that the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) dealt with; I did not go into that. I have no doubt that there is a very much longer and more interesting story with regard to this whole question than I am prepared to give in the time that is at my disposal now.
Of lard we imported 12,000,000, pounds and exported 8,000,000 pounds. Ever since the Canadian swine industry has been developed along the line of what we call the bacon type there has been a lessened production of lard. The fatter the animal is; the more it comes under the classification of " thick smooth," the less lard you will get from it, so that we need not be surprised if our lard importations increase as we develop the bacon type of hog for the British market. You cannot get it both ways; you cannot have a lean bacon type such as the foreign markets demand, and a fat animal at the same time. This is a good sign, because it is better to produce bacon than it
is to produce lard. Anybody can produce lard, but anybody cannot produce bacon.
Of bacon and hams, 6,000,000 pounds were imported and 99,000,000 pounds exported. There is a demand for the fat ham and the thicker bacon in certain markets throughout Canada, and that is imported because it is cheaper, while the other is exported because it caters to the more fastidious taste of the British market, which is prepared to pay the money for the good quality. That accounts for the difference between the import and the export.
Of fresh pork we imported 22,000,000 pounds and exported 1,000,000 pounds. This import, my information is, is to keep our abattoirs running during a shortage of live hogs on the Canadian market. They find it pays them better to import green pork from the United States, and thus keep the curing facilities going at the abattoir, than to close their packing plants; so that they make this import of green pork and then export the product. The pork is held in bond during the curing process.
Of pork in brine, we imported 9,000,000 pounds and exported only 430,000 pounds. This is the real, old-fashioned three or four inch thick stuff we used to see many years ago in the shanties. There was an idea that the shanty-men had lost their taste for this heavy meat and were demanding the tender cuts just like other people, but apparently there is still a considerable demand for it-so much so that we have not the supply to meet it and consequently we have had to import
9,000,000 pounds.
Of seed we imported nealy $4,000,000 worth and exported over $8,500,000 worth-over twice as much, so that the situation there is quite satisfactory. The seeds that we import are largely those that do not grow in Canada.

May I ask a question? Is it not a fact that many of our heavy hogs that make the kind of pork referred to are shipped to the United States instead of being used here in Canada? I know of one firm in I\etaskiwin, not far from Edmonton, that claimed to have made $6,000 by shipping just that kind of hog to the United States and then importing the finished product.

That is quite possible. [DOT] In more than one case Canadian butter and eggs have been shipped to the British market, and in a month or two have been shipped back to Canada. It is a case of overshipment to the British market, and before the new, fresh, winter eggs come in they find it commercially possible an^ feasible to"

The Buuyet-Mr. Motherwell
have them shipped back again. This frequently happens.
The matter of vegetables is frequently discussed by many, particularly our Conservative friends. I want to say quite frankly I have some sympathy with them on the question of vegetables, but when you know the record, it does not look so bad. We imported $3,900,000, nearly $4,000,000 worth of vegetables, and we exported almost the same, $3,700,000, or a difference of $200,000, so it very nearly balances.
Take raw wool. That looks like a reflection on our disposition to diversify and take advantage of all the opportunities on our farms. We imported 19,000,000 pounds, and we exported only 6,000,000 pounds. I think that is easy to explain. These are largely merino wools, the finer wools of Australia that our Canadian woollen factories desire in order to make the finer cloths. We have not the population to make use of all our own coarse wool, and our wool therefore goes to Boston and other United States points, where they have a large population and there is a large and varied demand for all qualities of wool. There is no reflection there such as was apparently desired to be thrown upon the agricultural development of Canada.
There are more of these things we can do. This last year the west alone has produced for export over 10,000,000 additional pounds of butter. The west will develop year by year until in a short time, inside of another ten or fifteen years, it will be exporting 100,000,000 pounds of creamery butter, judging by the rate they are going now. We are getting away from specialized farming, which is not a safety first system at all. Even eastern Canada can develop enormously along the lines of diversification. This old province of Ontario, with a little more attention to winter dairying and improving the quality of the cows, could in ten years double its butter output. We are just awakening to the fact that we have to pay more attention to all these things, and not buy any more than we can help of what we can grow profitably at home. You know quite a wave went over the country ten or fifteen years ago- Oh, it is not worth while bothering with these things. Let us do the things that our farm and the community are specially adapted for, let us specialize. There is a lot to be said for specialization, but when you are specializing in a particularly precarious article, subject to climatic conditions, where do you stand if this specialty, due to climatic conditions or other reasons, falls down? You have nothing left; We are entering an era when
fMr. Motherwell.]
people want to play safe. Why do we see such a tremendous development in our insurance business? People who were insured for $10,000 yesterday want $20,000 insurance to-day; people who were not insured at all yesterday are seeking insurance to-day. They want something that is safe. They do not want to make a big profit out of something, but simply to play safe. That is the result of the discipline we got in the debauch of the war period and for a year or two afterwards, and it is a good sign. We are also playing safe in agriculture by diversifying our farming, and it is a good sign; it is something to congratulate ourselves upon, rather than a reflection upon agriculture, because we find it convenient sometimes to export and sometimes to import. So much for that question.
I have been criticizing the official opposition for a short time-I usually do. I take far more delight in criticizing my regular traditional opponents, whose steel I always respect but whom I like, and I shall like them much better if we keep them just where they are, which it is our business to do. But just now I am under the necessity of criticizing my very good friend from Springfield (Mr. Hoey). I do not think enough attention is paid to him in this House. He is one of the most capable of the front benchers among our Progressive friends. Whenever he speaks he gives us a treat. Anybody, whether he is a literary man or not, who likes a well rounded speech, faultless rhetoric, beautiful sentences uttered in that rich Irish voice, which cannot be beat, cannot but be charmed by the hon. member for Springfield. I am not saying that for the purpose of paving the way for something terrible. I just wanted to point out that while his speech had all these beauties, it had also this danger, that it was misunderstood, I think, by some members of the House, and will be misunderstood by the country. There was not the point to it that seemed to lie on the surface. Take the eulogy, for instance, my hon. friend gave of Mr. Jones as a business man. It was deserving of Mr. Jones as a business man, but I am afraid Mr. Jones has been too much of a business man for my hon. friend. He was pretty nearly so for myself. I had the pleasure of being invited to the Country Club one night, on an occasion, when the honoured guest was Mr. Jones, the manager of the Cement Company, the institution that we have heard so much about, and whose profits a great many Progressives, particularly the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans), have complained so much about. I listened to Mr. Jones describing this uniform,

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
flat rate budget he was going to impose on the country, and unlike this formal occasion, his address was given informally around "* table, after the dinner had been done full justice to, and then afterwards we were privileged to sit in committee of the whole, as it were, and ask questions, and after we started asking questions and began to find out what this flat rate budget meant, I was amazed. This flat rate budget was going to raise not only $130,000,000 that the present budget provides for, but $120,000,000 more, making in all $250,000,000, to be raised by a tariff applied on a flat rate basis to everything that comes into 'Canada-nothing coming in free at all, but just a flat uniform tariff on everything. I think the hon. member for Springfield quite understood that, because he drew particular attention to it. Not only that, but when my colleague the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) mentioned it and asked the hon. member for Springfield if he was in favour of this "Jones'' policy- shall I call it, just as we speak of the Dawes plan-the hon. member for Springfield started out to say that when the government declared just what their position was in regard to the Jones policy he would be ready to declare his. I did not know that hon. members expected the government to declare itself on the Jones plan. Maybe they had heard of this dinner at the Country Club and expected we were going to take over the Jones plan as part of our policy. But my hon. friend from Springfield did not Stop there. He said:
I will state now without hesitation or equivocation-
Like a real Irishman he is afraid of nothing, he goes right to it:
-that Mr. Jones' policy would mean an immeasurably better tariff than we have at the present time.
That means a tariff whose good qualities cannot be measured as compared with ours; the Jones tariff was the best tariff the hon. member had in sight, immeasurably better than the present budget. Let us examine what the unequivocal statement means. It was also pointed out that the Jones plan would produce $250,000,000 of revenue, based on an importation of $800,000,000 worth of goods. Now anybody can take out his pencil and check up. The Jones flat rate tariff was to be levied on $800,000,000 worth of goods, and was to produce $250,000000 of revenue. Divide $250,000,000 by $800,000,000, and you will find you get a uniform flat rate duty of thirty-one and a fraction per cent. No wonder the cement merger would like that arrangement. This man, Mr. Jones, is not as easy as he looks; he gets, as near as I can figure out, not quite ten per cent protection
on cement. I did not know that at the time.
I innocently sat at the feet of Mr. Jones learning the new national policy. Now we are having another policy proposed which is intended to replace the old one. Well, 31 per cent was to be levied on everything on the free list and Mr. Jones says that two-fifths of the goods we need are imported free. Take binder twine. I would not care to go into the constituency of Springfield and advocate a duty of 31 per cent on binder twine; but apparently the hon. member for that constituency (Mr. Hoey) is prepared for such a policy in order that he may "keep up with the Joneses." I cannot understand that. I am in doubt as to whether the hon. gentleman understood what that policy involved. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that when my colleague asked the hon. member for Springfield whether he was speaking for the Progressive party he promptly said: "No, I am speaking for myself"; he was searching about for some betterment because he said "that the truth did sometimes come out of Nazareth," meaning in this instance, Montreal. So the rest of the Progressive party are in no way responsible for these statements and I am glad of that; I am sorry ever to have to criticize one of them. Here is a list of articles free of duty which I have prepared ; they are comprised in part of the first half of the alphabet, from a to m:
Animals for improvement of stock-ewes and lambs for breeding purposes.
Everybody knows that these animals come in free. The commoner stock does not come in free; it is now proposed to subject the pure bred stock to a duty of 31 per cent in the interest of the live stock industry of Canada.
Animal manures.
One of my hon. friends from a constituency near Montreal is always talking about the heinousness of allowing our barnyard fertilizers to go to the United States, and here is a proposition to apply a 31 per cent tariff to manures.
Antitoxin.
Think of the advantages now enjoyed by human beings. This is one of the greatest boons open to mankind and yet my genial hearted Irish friend wishes to tax it 31 per cent.
Apparel wearing, settlers'.
Like my hon. friend I am an immigrant only I moved from eastern Canada to the west; my hon. friend crossed the Atlantic to Canada. Our apparel now comes in free but my hon. friend would make it subject to a duty of 31 per cent.

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
Apparatus for boring and drilling for water, gas oil or minerals of a class or kind not made in Canada-
And so forth. This is now free, but my hon. friend would have it subject to a duty of 31 per cent.
Apparatus, and glass ware for laboratory work and sterilizing purposes for hospitals.
I never was in a hospital until I was forty-five years of age. I had thought it was a disgrace for a man or woman to be found in such an institution. Now, I think it is one of the greatest humanitarian agencies in existence, possibly outside of the Christian church. All these things are to be taxed although formerly they were free. " Keeping up with the Joneses " is a terrible game to play.
Artificial limbs and parts thereof.
Hon. gentlemen will remember last year when the public gallery of this chamber was full of members of the Amputation Association. We also heard them as on wooden legs they stumped down the corridors keeping time with military precision. All these limbs now come in free but under my hon. friend's plan they would meet	a duty of 31 per
cent.
Artificial teeth not mounted.
What is a man to do when he gets old and loses his molars and grinders? I am approaching that age. But my hon. friend wants to charge me 31 per cent. I shall either have to " gum " my food or pay 31 per cent.
Asbestos roofing cement.
A very necessary article in building operations in a new district. It will have to pay 31 per cent under my hon. friend's plan.
Augurs, coal mining machinery.
Where are my hon. friends from the Maritime provinces who are so greatly interested in the question of coal? Where are those hon. members who are so constant in urging that the cost of the implements of production be kept down? Here is a proposition to jack up the cost by 31 per cent.
Barbed fencing wire
Binder twine.
I remember how in the good old Liberal days of Sir Wilfrid Laurier we made the welkin ring when we got binder twine and barbed wire on the free list. Our modern reformer, however, wants to place these under a duty of 31 per cent. I am going to exonerate my hon. friend from the responsibility for this; I think he must have been teetotal'ly mesmerized. I sympathize with him because I was almost lured into the same boat. How-

ever, I went further into a study of the figures; I am Scotch and blest with a saving streak which my hon. friend has not got.

Does the hon. minister remember at the time the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) made the comparison between the Jones plan and the present budget it was before the latest amendment to the dumping act had been brought down?

Oh, no, it was not, and anyhow the dumping act has nothing to do with this particular question; it is a matter which stands by itself.
Boards, sawn etc., dressed on one side only, sawn, or split only.
Books, namely books on the application of science to industries of all kinds, including books on agriculture, horticulture, forestry and so on.
When people want to know a little more about agriculture, horticulture and forestry and wish to import works on these subjects from any part of the globe they will not be free to do so without paying a duty of 31 per cent.
Bowls for cream separators, steel.
Cream separators.
That was another thing good Sir Wilfrid got for us, but my hon. friend is seeking to put it back at 31 per cent.
Coals, briquettes, anthracite, cutting machines, except percussion coal cutters.
How will the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) be able to carry out his briquetting proposition when my Progressive friend from Springfield gets a duty of 31 per cent placed on anthracite?
The minister is talking about 31 per cent duty. Who is advocating that?

Well, that is the
Jones' plan.

I defy the minister to quote
any such thing from Mr. Jones' statement.
I will have to quote the figures again.
I defy you to quote any such thing from Mr. Jones' statement.

I am just brushing aside the rhetorical phrases and letting the statement stand out in bold, naked outline. My hon. friend from Springfield in his speech a few days ago declared:
But I will state now without hesitation or equivocation that Mr. Jones' policy would mean an immeasurably better tariff than we have at the present time.

Hear, hear.

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell

That is what my
hon. friend himself said. Now I will quote what Mr. Jones said:
From a revenue standpoint our tariff is a complete failure. I am not going into details, but our importations into Canada, in round figures, are a billion dollars per year. In 1921 our imports reached $1,240,000,000, in 1922 they dropped to $774,000,000, in 1923 they were $802,000,000, so that they are now on the up grade.
Then my hon. friend from Springfield makes this comment:
Mr. Jones goes on to advocate what he calls a uniform tariff not only on manufactured goods entering the country, but on raw material as well, which revision he claims would bring an added amount of revenue into treasury of approximately $120,000,000.
And my hon. friend says that such a tariff would be immeasurably better than ours. He does not say what his plan is, but he accepts that as the best he can think of. It is the production of one of the super-men who is summoned to our aid.
Will the minister tell us where Mr. Jones advocated a 31 per cent tariff.
He did not go that far. That is why he pretty nearly caught some people.
Hear, hear.

No, he did not go
that far. His estimate, as far as I can recall it, was about 25 per cent. He did not figure it out minutely apparently, nor did I. But I take this document and this is what I am going by now. I assume they were all in a proper frame of mind at the dinner referred to, but it is safer to take the actual document.

The minister refers to a
dinner. The speech I quoted was given before the students of McGill University.
That does not make any difference.
There was no dinner.

It makes no difference. I say I had the pleasure of hearing Mr. Jones at the dinner mentioned at the Country Club. If he did not quote it properly at the university, I may say it is almost item by item the same speech I heard. It must be a favourite speech of his. No, that explanation will not go. Then we have coal, heading machines and we have crutches and1 specially constructed staffs for the cripples. I won my first election on crutches, and I have great sympathy for those who have to use them. I got my leg broken in the campaign and I did not wish to stand. It was the best vote-getter I ever had. Then we have:
Furnaces blast for copper or nickel.
Hemp seed for agricultural purposes.
I remember when we were making strenuous efforts to establish a hemp factory in Winnipeg, my hon. friend (Mr. Hoey) could not see his way to support it, but actually spoke against it. Now he does not want the seed to come in free. What are we to do? I thought we had a real, genuine Cobden talk from the hon, member for Brome (Mr. McMaster). Sometimes we fail to be able to follow his speech in its entirety, but we have to respect the old teachings. The teachings of our forefathers were great, but when you apply them in all their logical details they are a terror. Now if hon. members have any tears, prepare to shed them now.
Hymn books and Bibles.
These are on the free list. It is now proposed to make the duty on them 31 per cent. Cut that in two and make it fifteen if you will, The hon. member who has so creditably filled the pulpit for so many years cannot be accused of wanting to make the way to the celestial city more difficult. I think we will retire to-night with free Bibles and free hymn books, and if the Jones plan were to be followed we would wake up tomorrow with a taxation. Maybe we would think more of them if we did not get them so easily. Then the next item:
Machines, ditching (traction) (not being ploughs) adapted for tile drainage on farm.
That was another thing in Ontario that they wanted. They wished to get ditching machines, and you cannot get away from this. I have thought this out. Blood is thicker than water. I am always drawn to an Irishman, at the same time I like to have a little round out of him if he deserves it. And I think my hon. friend has been led away by this Jones plan. A flat rate would be a delightfully simple measure. I am sure the Acting Minister of Finance would not mind continuing his occupation if 'he could say, "Put it on a flat basis and we will be through with it." Hon. gentlemen will recall that when out in the west land was very cheap; a certain number of cents tax per acre was placed on it. The Minister of the Interior will recall that. It amounted to about five dollars on a quarter-section. It was very easy, -but when land became valuable, and people insisted on land values being taxed, in order to have any uniformity in the taxes, we found it necessary to provide for an assessment. A flat rate would be delightfully simple. We would be able to tax all raw material, whether hemp, tobacco, cotton or anything else. This

The Budget-Mr. Mothervrell
is the scheme to be followed out under Mr. Jones' modern plan of taxation. You cannot get away from it. I wish somebody would help me get away from it.
The Minister of Agriculture is giving the House a wrong impression altogether.
Correct me if I am wrong. I will sit down for half an hour while you explain how I am wrong, and if I am wrong I will retract.

The hon. minister is giving
a wrong impression to the House. Mr. Jones' words were that eighty per cent of the imports are coming in now for the already privileged class. He is not speaking of a one hundred per cent tariff on one hundred per cent of the goods coming in, but on eighty per cent, which is already coming in to the privileged class.

Does anybody
understand that? There is something wrong somewhere. I cannot understand it at all. I have got the wrong .scent, or else my hon. friend who has just asked a question is on the wrong track.

Will my hon. friend read
the words himself?

I am in the middle of a speech. I do not say this defiantly, but here is a magnificent speech broadcasted all over western Canada, made by one of the most capable men in the House, and I say the statement should be corrected. The Acting Minister of Finance brought down the budget speech. It does not matter where the document came from. It is my duty to defend the budget. If it were my brother or my father it would be my duty to defend it, and consequently my hon. friend' from Springfield will not misunderstand me. He has not a greater admirer in this House than myself. I have never made a practice of taking advantage of anybody in the House. I will give hon. gentlemen an opportunity to explain, and nobody would take advantage of my sitting down and saying I am through with my speech, because I am not. I have only got to "M" in the list, and that is only the middle of the alphabet. There are hundreds of articles on the free list. Suppose we go to an excess in the matter of charitableness and say Mr. Jones only meant it was to apply to $130,000,000 of revenue-that he only meant that the present amount of revenue was to be raised. That will be sixteen per cent, or about half. If you like we will take it that way. But I do not see 
that we could do that, because the hon. member for Springfield adopted the statement right off the bat. Now what about the articles in the tariff that caused my good friends from Brantford (Mr. Raymond), North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) and St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) so much worry. Some of us had to sweat blood to get those duties reduced. Hon. members understand that when you get something by hard labour you do not- let it slip away from your fingers. Here is a list of articles	running	from	six	per cent to tenper cent usually. That is pretty low. You cannot	call that	a protective tariff. Underthe Jones plan	that	has	to be raised towhichever you like now. If they only meant	that we	were	to	raise the $130,-
000,000 which we raise at present, and which they described as no revenue at all to come from the tariff we should have, that means sixteen per cent. If it is to be $250,000,000 it means thirty-one per cent, whichever you like. You pay your money and you take your choice. It makes no difference here. But here is the thing that hurts me more than anything else, because this was in my own time, and the Acting Minister of Finance understands the difficulty we had in getting some of these things. Then we have the item:
Grain binders.
I can remember when they were pretty nearly thirty-one per cent. Then we have:
Drills, mowing machines, cultivators, threshing machines.
I remember when the duty on threshing machines was 35 per cent. The duties on these are all less than 10 per cent now. Last year the Progressive party thought that the budget was not bad and they supported it, the only budget which they have supported in the last three years. The first two budgets they did not support, but they supported the budget last year, thus showing that as a party ! they confirmed it. But the hon. member for Springfield was not speaking for them; he made it quite plain that he was asking nobody to accept responsibility for his statement, and I want my hon. friends to understand that I am not asking them to accept responsibility for this because I am dealing with just the hon. member for Springfield now. These items are to be raised to a uniform tariff, after all the struggle, all the effort we went through to bring the duty down. This gentleman, Mr! Jones, is a business man, in the firm that produces the Beaverbrooks, and apparently you cannot produce them on a 9 per cent ad valorem duty. The duty is a specific one, but working it

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
out as an ad valorem duty, it comes to around 9 per cent. As I say, you cannot produce them apparently on a 9 per cent ad valorem duty and he would much prefer to have it 30 per cent. He has little dinners here and there and he unfolds a plan that, on the face of it, looks like a crackerjack, but which is meant to be something to make Beaver-brooks out of. That is the situation. I will sit down right now if the hon. member wants to question my statement, as I am not bluffing at all.
Before the minister gets away from that, will he tell us what the rate of duty is on bituminous slack that he is supporting in the present budget? I think it works out a little over 50 per cent.

It is a specific
duty. I suppose some of them would come down, but look at the number that go up.
Coal would come down anyway.
We are not all manufacturers interested in bituminous slack.
What about automobiles?

There must be
something on the other side of the ledger or the thing wrould certainly be a fierce frost. It is certainly a frost enough. I find another remarkable coincidence in regard to this matter. Three years ago when the Minister of the Interior was wrestling with his estimates on immigration hard and long into the night after five full days-and it was the morning of the sixth day before he got even one item through-I recall this fact because it is connected with cement-my good friend got up and advocated very ably that this government should introduce a scheme somewhat similar to the one which the old government introduced. He mudt have thought more of them than he does now. He wanted this government to adopt a housing plan for farm labourers in Canada, east or west or all over, similar to the housing plans of the cities which housing plans we were glad to drop. The buildings were to be made of concrete, indestructible, and worth $2,500 apiece. Labourers are certainly "some pumpkins" nowadays if you are going to build houses of that character for them on a farm when the farmer himself has a shack worth not a quarter of that amount. But we shall let that pass. Concrete is made out of broken stone, more or less coarse gravel and cement, but the greatest of all is cement. Keeping up with the Joneses! Keeping in with the Joneses, apparently! What a remarkable coincidence! I want to exonerate my hon. friend from anything associated with this at all. It is a purely extraordinary coincidence that he should advocate the construction of all these cement houses at a cost of $2,500 apiece, and then come down and advocate a tariff running up to 30 per cent. This Jones business is getting on my nerves. I am very fortunate I did not fall for it myself and I am just as sympathetic to my hon. friend because he fell for it. I think he was tempted. This is the explanation of the whole thing and it is easy. An Irishman is said never to be at a loss for an answer. A Scotchman, in this case the Acting Minister of Finance was one too many for the Irishman-sometimes they will get the better of them, but very seldom-and he up and asked the hon. member if he was in favour of this Jones proposition. The hon. member had to think quickly and he said: "When the government declared where they were." He knew that was absolutely no answer at all, but it gave him time to think, and in my opinion, he should have taken a little more time to think. I do not accept his answer without reservation, but he said: "It is immeasurably better than the plan we have." He cannot get away from that. He was desirous of keeping up his well known Irish characteristic of being always ready with an answer for the faith that was in him. but that time he failed, and that was all. He is one of the most honourable men in this House and a man to be admired, but that kind of devilment gets out and hurts the government, and I am one of the government.
That completes, Mr. Speaker, the first half of my remarks. Might I ask that half-time be called?
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Hon. J. A. Robb (Acting Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to go into committee of Ways and Means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Sir Henry Drayton.
Hon. W. R, MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):	For some reason or other the
country generally, including the press, seem to be of the opinion that we are on the eve of a general election. Speaking for myself

I do not see very many signs of an election, but the impression is there nevertheless.
I can however discern some signs of an impending election in the fact that a great many of our friends in both opposing groups are apparently busy attending to their line fences. That is of course a quite legitimate 'business to engage in, and it may account for Some of the speeches that are being made and the resolutions that are being proposed in this House. I am going to refer to one line fence indication now of a more pleasing nature. Our friends immediately opposite have 'been taking care recently of one line fence, in the amendment to the budget. I have not the amendment before me, but if I remember rightly it makes little if any reference whatever to the tariff; although our friends have been talking diligently of protection ever since the 'budget was introduced. It would seem therefore that they have two .policies, one for the country outside, appearing in a manifesto issued through the press on January 4, a manifesto so-called, and distributed broadcast all over the country for outside consumption, 'and a second policy, more .carefully worded in the amendment to the budget, apparently for the consumption of the House.
I do not know what effect it is having on our Progressive friends, 'but even supposing that it avoids protection it evidently has no attraction for them.
I have here a clipping from t'he Montreal Star entitled:
Meighen demands tariff revision and commission. Broad policy of Conservative party outlined by leader. Save resources. Would make preferences conditional on use of Canadian ports.
Then is outlined a manifesto which I think I am justified in dealing with at this time inasmuch as it indicates, in some respects at least, far more plainly than does the amendment to the budget, the .policy of the Conservative party. In this it is distinctly stated that the intention is to resurrect protection in all its various forms and ramifications. That is the centre of the whole manifesto; it aims to restore protection such as Sir John A. Macdonald preached and such as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) now advocates; it is going to restore and bring back to life that form of protection. Well, it reminds me of one of t'he Sacred stories in [DOT] Holy Writ in which the dry bones, strewn in the valley, will by the divine hand be restored to life. You will observe, Mr. Speaker, that it took the divine hand to do that. The bones were brought joint to joint and marrow to marrow, were clothed with muscle and flesh, and then covered over with skin and made to stand up and look like men.

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
Now my hon. friends are going to restore a number of obsolete things like protection. They are going to restore the old nostrum that they have been prescribing for the last twenty-five years; and a preference for preference is outlined here. Well, preference for preference means no British preference. And they are going to build up Canadian ports; that is another one. They are going to build up Canadian ports by shipping in goods under the British preference, although there will be none. Besides, they are two_years late, even if they had that policy. The Minister of Finance adopted a policy two years ago whereby ten per cent addition was made to the British preference, but with the proviso that to obtain the advantage of it the goods must come in by Canadian ports. Under that policy 99g per cent of the dutiable goods from Great Britain coming under the British preference come in by Canadian ports, leaving seven-eighths subject to the reforms of my hon. friends on the other side who are not in favour of a preference at all. Dry bones to be restored? Let us see some more, now.
My hon. friends are to have a 'tariff board, composed of what, Mr. Speaker? Composed of representatives of the manufacturers, of the farmers and of labour. Theoretically fine, but it, really is surprising that a practical man like the right hon. leader of the opposition should be indulging in vagaries and fancies like this. Just imagine; we have been trying this for thirty years-I mean in a private way; many a time the proposal has been made in good faith, and acted upon, that the manufacturers .and the farmers especially should get together and try to evolve a tariff that would be congenial and pleasant to both. It is utterly impossible, in my estimation; yet such is the personnel of the board that my right hon. friend would establish to look over the tariff, to revise the tariff, to make recommendations to the cabinet. Labour is to be represented, too; whether or not that will, make it any easier I do not know. Well, you might as well take a dog and a cat, tie their tails together and hang them over the clothes line and expect harmony. I do not contend that the thing is impossible; I believe it would be a fine thing to aim at. But we have been aiming at it for a long while and we have failed. It is something like the shipping proposition; they have been aiming at a lot of things in the past and they have got us nowhere, and they want to keep on aiming at them. That is another dry bone that they want to restore, to endow with flesh and blood and sinew, and then to breathe into it the breath of life and make it stand up and look like something.
Well, it cannot be done-not by the human hand at least, and no other hand is likely to intervene at this time for this particular purpose.

Now, here is the funny part of it: when you get these three parties represented on a congenial body of this kind, and protection is handed out under their auspices, then-will the Progressives listen to this?-if anyone takes unfair advantage of the protection given, this body will report the fact to my right hon. friend-that is, when my hon. friends opposite get into power, which is something I do not think we need be alarmed about to-night. But when they get into power this unfair advantage will be reported and the protection will be withdrawn. Why, you might as well set a man before a good meal and say that if he takes advantage of it the meal will be taken away! Is that not What protection is for, to be taken advantage of? What is the good of it, as some hon. gentleman over there asked the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) this afternoon, if they do not take advantage of it? There are occasions when protection can go so far as to retain the market, in a measure, and the full advantage of it is sometimes taken; and occasionally the other party to the contract assumes the cost of protection.
