speechtext:
WThat did the right hon. gentleman say? I thought he promised to be good. Anyway, that is one more dry bone. Unfair advantage? We have heard of it for at least fifty years, and now it is restored, resurrected, renovated, rejuvenated, but by the hand of man only.
Now then, here we have another boneyard exhibit. My hon. friends make this proposal :
That to enable the products of the western and Maritime provinces to reach more readily the markets so developed the special transportation burdens borne by those provinces should be shared by the whole Dominion either by contribution to long haul freight costs or by assistance in some other form.
And this coming from the right hon. leader of the opposition! He is going to assist the Maritimes by some special contribution that is to be provided by the whole of Canada. That, I say, from the same gentleman who did his best to remove the advantages that the western provinces were enjoying under the Crowsnest pass agreement. In fact, he did suspend it for three years, and when we restored part of it he opposed the measure tooth and nail in this House. Last year when he went -through the western provinces he said again that he was opposed to it; it was not right; it was not fair that the eastern people should have their freight rates controlled by the railway commission while those of the west were controlled to some extent by act of parliament. Now he comes down at this eleventh hour and says: "We want some special consideration for the Maritime prov-

inces, and we want the rest of the people to pay for it." I am not objecting to the principle; I simply want to get at the cause of this sudden conversion. There is another phase of it: the intercolonial rates that the Maritime provinces had were tantamount to a little "crow" of their own down there until my right hon. friend took them away in the consolidation of that road with the National railways. There is a slight increase, I understand, over the old low rates in the present day consolidated rates under the Canadian National. But my right hon. friend and his government-or i-t may have been under his former leader, Sir Robert Borden, I do not recall-took away the special privileges and the special rates which complied, I believe with the spirit of the understanding under which the Maritime provinces entered the confederation. Now the hon. gentleman and his party come along in this mealy-mouthed fashion and ask an opportunity to give them back. Too late. Why do they talk that way? Oh, their bones are dry and their hope is gone, and they are going back to wallow in protection again. Well, it cannot be done. Protection is not all gone yet; I do not know whether we will ever live to see it all abolished; it may not be possible to do away with it all, it may not be desirable; but at all events we do not want the brand of protection my right hon. friend and his party preach. So much for these relics, so much for this valley of bones. They seem sad over the impending fate of Canada. It is business depression that is preached bv the hon. member'for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion). It hangs over us, according to him, about as thick as a London fog. As a matter of fact, a little introspection will show us that the depression is in 'the Tory prospects in this country; that is where the -depression has been ever since their defeat in the second battle of Hastings. Their spirits have been getting lower and lower ever since, and the last -tiling they want is an election. I do not know that anybody in this House is particularly pining for an election. People do not look for this heavy expense and turmoil before they have to. The regular term of parliament is five years. Why should we add twenty per cent to the cost of that by bringing on an election every four years? That is what the -man in the street may be saying. The hearts of hon. gentlemen opposite, as a matter of -fact, are frozen for fear an election might come. , Hence the depression.

speechtext:
If my hon. friend
looks after his seat I will 'look after mine. I may say candidly I do not know where it will be, but I have had four or five seats offered to me. I do not know how many more there will be before the time comes.
As I was pointing out, Mr. Speaker, there was a time when hon. gentlemen opposite wanted an election, and that was a little over a year ago. I think they would have welcomed one at the end of our first year here, when we were sweltering 'between two forces that were grinding us to pieces, the Cavil Service Commission and the upper chamber. My hon. friends were ready to jump in then and take advantage of our apparent helplessness. Last year, when they thought they had something terrible on three or four members of this government, maligning them and libelling them as anything but honest men, they would have liked to go into the country; in fact, they went to the country themselves in West Hastings, and they would have 'liked to go to the country all over Canada. But I am not going to bring out all the harrowing details of that disaster which they 'brought on themselves; but that is when they wanted an election, and they got- it. They do not want one now, and no amount of bluff will prevail on me to believe they do. They are not ready. As a matter of fact, who is ready? But they are the least ready, Mr. Speaker, in the whole House. Now I think I am through with the valley of bones. We will have to get Ezekiel on the job if my hon. friends hope to resurrect all this dry timber and manufacture something out of it that will look like new.
Now, I have got in wrong with one of the Progressives at least, and I presume I have got in wrong with all the Conservatives. That is my luck. I suppose I am going to get in wrong with some of my own friends. I am going to talk now a little about two things, the Hudson Bay railway and the St. Lawrence route.
I was not an ardent advocate of the Hudson Bay railway until last year. This is a work that the people of western Canada have been looking for and sighing for and waiting for, for forty years. Sometimes our friends down here think we are not just right on that question, that we are a little bit sprung on it. Let me point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that ever since trade has been established between the nations, go away back to the early history of mankind, if you like, and you will find that people have sought the sea for the purpose of trade. That was the cheapest way to 124i
transport their goods, rather than by the com-bersome and expensive caravans travelling overland in those days. It is the inherited instinct of the human race to seek the shortest cut to tidewater in their endeavour to trade with other nations, and we are only exhibiting what is bred and born in us, that inherent instinct in the human race, in seeking this access to tidewater. The Dominion of Canada has committed itself to this work-both parties, all parties, if you like, in this House. Take a compass, if you can imagine one long enough, with one prong in the city of Regina and the other in Fort William, and then swing it around and it will land you at Port Nelson. Therefore, when you ship a cargo of goods from the west to Fort William, it is the same distance to take those goods to Port Nelson, and that route is 1,000 miles nearer the market than if you shipped them by Montreal. Do not blame us, Mr. Speaker, for entertaining these hopes. I remember less than fifteen years ago everybody smiled at the thought of Vancouver being a port through which to send our products to the Old Country via the Panama canal. The first article I ever read on the subject was by the present Senator Laird, and I thought he was plumb bug-house when I read it. Everybody told you the water was so warm down there that the wheat travelling that route would be all heated and fermented, and experts were sent with thermometers to test the wheat in transit. Well, anybody who knows anything about conduction knows perfectly well that heat and cold are not conducted in a granular body like wheat or sand. And now the complaint is made with regard to the Hudson bay route that that is too cold. Some people are never pleased. I have been studying the whole situation, and I want to say that so far as my judgment goes there is no more chance of failure in the building of the Hudson bay route than there was in the building of the Panama canal, or of the Suez canal, or in the building of the Canadian Pacific railway. Why should there be?
I am not going to deal with the question of when the Hudson Bay railway should be completed, because that matter is already in a resolution on the order paper. I would point out, however, this similarity. You remember the story, Mr. Speaker, of Christopher Columbus when he set sail some years ago, I do not, remember just when, to cross the uncharted Atlantic, and when he arrived about the same distance across the Atlantic as we are towards Hudson bay, that is eighty per cent, his muntinous crew wanted him to turn back, but Columbus persevered

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
and landed on this continent. Well now, there are, I will not say mutinous, but fainthearted Canadians who want us to turn back now we are four-fifths of the way to Hudson bay. Is that the kind of stuff we are made of? Does that in Canadians mean ambition? Ambition should be made of sterner stuff than that. Surely the country that built the Canadian Pacific railway across the lake region and the prairies and over the mountains should not falter at completing the Hudson Bay railway some time. I can only put it that way in respect to the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Knox) and his resolution. This was a matter of public concern away back in Hugh Sutherland's time, over forty years ago, before the Canadian Pacific was built. As a matter of fact, it was in those early days that we got the real views of experts on the question. No other influences governed them, there were no other influences to govern them. Information was available on the question, and I am going to read some of that information after a while.
What I want to point out is this:	Just
as the Liberal party was the party to turn the first sod in the building of the Canadian Pacific railway under government construction, so the Liberal government under Sir Wilfrid Laurier was the first government to commence the building of the Hudson Bay railway. They started to build it in 1910, and were continuing the work in 1911; I remember there was only one constituency that went Conservative at that time. That [DOT]was the year of the reciprocity treaty, and the reason that constituency went Conservative was because we were not, in its opinion, building that railway fast enough. I refer to the constituency of Prince Albert. When the Conservatives came in for good or for ill- we will say it was for good; we will have to take it that way anyway-when they came into power, to their credit, I think, they took the right course. The Minister of Railways of that time went on a tour through the Hudson bay district and around to Nelson. He came back and apparently reported favourably on the project because the then government went on building the line; we must give everyone his due. The bridge over the Kettle river was built by the preceding government; and then the subsequent government-Union government, Conservative government, hybrid government, or National Liberal and Conservative government; you know the one I mean, the one with the long name, longer than you can remember, that is the one-went on with the enterprise.

Well now, the country is committed to the project; there is no use in discussing at this late date the practicability of the Hudson bay route. Over 100 years ago the Selkirk settlers entered Canada that way. That was their route to the western plains-it was not by railway that they hoped to go in there

and people had been going in that way for 250 years. Why, there were fortifications on Prince of Wales island, at the mouth of Churchill river, equal almost to the fortifications at Quebec. They were splendid fortifications. When they were built they were built with an eye to the future. People believed in the route at that time. Then, look at the primitive sailing vessels of that day without any radio, without any fog horns, without any lights, or any of the aids to navigation such as we have to-day all along the St. Lawrence. Under those conditions, with comparatively few facilities, the primitive sailing vessels of that day followed that route for 250 years. Nowadays, we have modern steamships and all possible aids to navigation, and they do not need to run into ice jams. The ocean there is the same Atlantic that laves the shores of old England, it is an arm of the Atlantic, a bay and a strait that never freeze, in the sense that we understand the term and are jammed full of ice only for a comparatively short period. Well then, why do we fear? The question of the practicability of this route was decided long ago. The only question now before the country is when can we afford to build the line? I suppose, if I were to be quite (candid, that if either the Hudson Bay railway or the Welland canal were mooted to-day for the first time, it is very unlikely that either would be commenced just at this period. But both enterprises have been started, we have got to take things as we find them; and it is very important to get the Welland canal finished. We have a big sum in the estimates for that purpose, and rightly so. But there are not enough of us in this House who think the Hudson Bay railway should be finished. Now, the reason I am saying this, and appealing to my hon. friends on this side particularly, is because I listened, with great interest, to the speech of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-8t. George (Mr. Marler)-in the debate on the Address. I have watched that young man ever since he came to the House. Sometimes, he stumbles a bit from my standpoint, but he is groping for the truth, he is a true Canadian, and he is trying to evolve a balanced policy for Canada. Some weeks ago I noted some press reports of a speech made

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
by the hon. member and I asked him for a copy of that speech the other day and he gave me one. From a careful reading of the speech so far as I can understand, his heart's desire is that the strong should bear the burdens of the weak, and by reason of the dissimilarity of interests that exist, where the tariff is burdensome on a weak, outlying province, then Canada as a whole should come to the relief of that province. My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition is just coming to a realization of that policy but I am afraid he is too late. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George is preaching the policy of equalization; preaching the policy that if you cannot treat all the provinces alike do something else by way of compensation. Although I do not think that I shall succeed as well as he did I am going to endorse the same principle.
I ask for the sympathetic consideration of members of this House on behalf of those of us in the west who are looking to get to tidewater by the shortest possible route. Now. I want hon. members to keep an open mind on this question. Personally I have gone up as far as the Kettle rapids on the Hudson bay route. I did not go to Nelson river; I had an engagement in Winnipeg and the trip that far would have occupied two or three weeks longer. Consequently I could not go there as I would like to have done. I suppose I do not know as much about the facilities of Nelson harbour as I should have if I had gone there and seen the harbour for myself. I am not a maritime man and do not pretend to know much about ports; I do know however, that some of them cost quite a little money. What information I have has been gathered from navigators, engineers, fishermen, settlers and trappers. I do not know why we are not now going to Churchill instead of going to Nelson, and I am going to read and1 put on Hansard some of the authorities whose testimony makes that question still more puzzling. Again I ask, in view of what these authorities say, why did they go to Nelson? I do not know. Some of our western friends are impatient on this subject, and I do not blame them because they have really been thwarted on this matter so long. I do not blame the late government for suspending work in 1917 and 1918. I recognize that I run the risk of being misunderstood in casting doubt on the practicability of Nelson as a proper harbour. I have come to the conclusion that there has been a big blunder made in going to Nelson. Why did they dP it? Who am I that I should presume to have information on that point?
Well, I am going to quote what was stated in an annual report of the Department of the Interior in 1884:
The Nelson, in the last thirty miles of its course expands like a funnel, from half a mile to many miles in width at its mouth so that it offers no natural advantages or facilities for a harbour, but rather the reverse.
Why should we fight against nature? If we get nature on our side, all the forces of nature, it will be like going down hill with the wind at our backs; but fighting against nature is a different thing. When I passed through St. John I did not see Courtenay bay which is washed by the Fundy tides. That work is taking quite a lot of dredging. I have heard a lot about it but did not see the locality myself; I came through at night and took sail early in the morning. When I compare Nelson to Courtenay bay I do not know to which I am doing an injustice; but I think it will involve interminable dredging to keep open the channel of the Nelson as it enters Hudson bay. Now I quote from the report of the government expedition under Lieutenant Gordon in 1886:
I consider the estuary of the Nelson river is one of the most dangerous places in the - world for shipping
to go.
What evil spirit directed our people to Nelson instead of Churchill where people have been going for over 250 years, where there is a land-locked harbour with a narrow entrance of less than half a mile, and with deep water; and if you want to enlarge it, it will take care of our shipping for a considerable length of time, being capable of being enlarged with comparative ease.
Lieut. Gordon continues:
I can only repeat my previously expressed opinion that the Nelson harbour is no port, nor would the expenditure of any amount of money make it a desirable place for shipping.
If you wanted to queer this project you would shoot it into Nelson, and that is as far as it would go. Captain Bernier is one of the living apostles who gives evidence. I would like to meet him, but am sorry to say I never did. I believe he was in Ottawa a short time ago. He is a sailor and no theorist, a practical mariner, an explorer, a man who goes north every year or almost every year on Arctic expeditions. He knows what ice is and realizes what danger is. He has been captain of a vessel since he was seventeen years of age. I understand that in middle life he thought there was more money in farming. He tried it, but he is back now on the sea. Perhaps he was unfortunate. If we keep our business in hand I say that there are worse occupations than farming. Here is what Captain Bernier says:

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
In the Hudson bay, as far as my experience has gone, there are two ports-Port Nelson, which will never be a port, because the river gives so much sediment and every spring when there is a heavy thaw there is a wash-out which changes the channel of the previous year. Therefore, a vessel coming in would need to have full knowledge of the present spring before she could enter, and she might be obliged to discharge outside. I consider that Canada is too poor to maintain a port like Nelson.
Listen to this:
I consider Canada is too poor to maintain a port like Nelson.

speechtext: What date is that?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That statement was made before the Roj^al Grain Commission in 1923 by Captain Bernier. Now, what about the engineers? I do not want to reflect upon the engineers, but after reading this evidence I will explain what I thiink the situation is:
At Nelson you have to build on sand or make foundation.
Hon. members know what happens to a foundation built on sand. Then he refers to Dr. Bell.
The difficulty of mapping the shore accurately is increased by the fact that the sea is receding at an appreciable rate.
It is shallow there. It is a tidal harbour with a very low tide, and they have to discharge their cargoes there. It has two advantages which I will deal with later. One does not count but the other does.
Mr. Joseph Robson, the surveyor of the Hudson's Bay Company reported:
Monday, the 15th July, 1745, fifteen minutes past seven in the morning, set sail in the factory's long boat, in company with Capt. Fowler, from on board the Sea-horse pink, then lying in Five-fathom hole, to sound and discover Port Nelson river. At thirty-eight minutes past seven, abreast of the beacon that stands at Five-fathom hole, the water fallen one foot, a neap tide, wind N.E., fresh gale.

At sixteen minutes past ten we had three fathom water; being on the north side of the sand that parts the fairway into the two rivers Nelson and Hayes.
And then, he goes on and says.
We cut our names on the trees in the N.E. end of Seal island.
From eight fathom and a half we stood to the S. eastward about three miles, saw a point or ridge of stones on the south side, distance about three-quarters of a mile, sounded three fathoms; this point of stone dries three or four feet perpendicular and seems to lie two or three miles from shore; but there are flats that dry at low water all the way to the shore, so that a man may walk from these stones to the land.
This indicates that in the estimation of these gentlemen who are practical men, perhaps not engineers and may not know much about the theory of engineering, the project is practicable. These men are doing things and giving us a real opinion, and are like

Captain Bernier in this respect; no matter what engineers say, he has done it himself. What he knows he tells under oath before the Royal Grain Commission. What I have been reading is against Port Nelson, but here is something in favour of Fort Churchill, written by Sir Henry Lefroy, secretary of the British Geographical Association:
It (Churchill) will undoubtedly be the future shipping port for the agricultural products of the vast Northwest territory, and the route by which immigrants will enter the countiy.
In Lord Selkirk's time that is the way they came through:
They wintered . at a point between Kettle rapids and Nelson, proceeding to the Red river settlement in the spring. That was before the Canadian Pacific railway was built. Nobody thinks of going in that way, we do not have to, but it just shows they saw a vision of an entrance into the northwest via Hudson bay, a great arm of the Atlantic.
Dr. Bell, Director Geological Survey of Canada, in an address to the Royal Geographical Society, October, 1881-that is the year the Canadian Pacific railway contract was entered into says:
The Churchill river is remarkable for having at its mouth a splendid harbour, with deep water and every natural convenience for the purposes of modern commerce.
Ask a pilot on the St. Lawrence or a pilot anywhere what he wants. He will tell you good deep water and good coast line. He does not want to go any place where he has to hold1 his breath for fear of bumping on the rocks below. Then George A. Bayne, civil engineer, gave evidence before the Royal Grain Commission as follows:
The harbour of Churchill is one of the finest I have ever seen. Nature has done so much for it in the way of protection from storm and the depth of water, that without further improvements it is fitted to take rank among first-class ocean ports.
Mark that
It is fitted to take rank among the first ocean ports.
That means that it is fitted to take rank with Montreal, Quebec, Halifax and St. John. Why do we fear? What is going to happen if we have one more ocean port? Will anything but good happen to us?
Mr. William Smith Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries, in an article in the Nautical Magazine, August, 1892, said:
"Stone lies at the water's edge ready to be laid into the docks or piers, and nature seems to have left little to be done to make this a capacious port, capable of doing business on a large scale, and, what is of the greatest importance, an inlet by Hudson bay is the only thoroughly independent channel which can ever be established between Great Britain and her north American possessions. ' '
The only channel? I wonder is that true? Let us see how our grain goes now. I know that I never realized till last summer that we are dependent on a friendly foreign nation

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
for every carload of grain which leaves Canada for Europe. If it goes via Vancouver it must go through the Panama canal, over which we have no control. I think there is some international arrangement, but hon. members know what happens to such arrangements. I am not fearful that they are going to be disturbed, but I have pointed out that the grain that goes west does not go through an independent channel, but through a splendid canal built by our friends to the south, and every bushel of grain that comes from Port Arthur and Fort William and goes down to Montreal and Buffalo has to go through the American Sault at Sault Ste. Marie. Why? Because the Canadian Sault is not sufficiently deep for the large vessels of the upper lakes or for any of these vessels. I was there last summer and I found that our boats drawing grain came down the American Sault. Consequently, strictly speaking, right off the bat, it is true, as has been stated, and no equivocation, that this is the only independent route worth speaking of, from the great plains of the west to the outside world. I do not think we will ever have any difficulty about it. I say to our friends from Montreal and from Quebec that we are all proud of those ports, and the better we do the better they do, but what makes Montreal great? It is the great fertile country that she serves.
Let me read this report about Churchill:
A harbour such as that of Churchill on Hudson bay would have the advantage over Quebec or Montreal of connecting directly with the open sea, and here in the autumn vessels would not, be liable to be frozen in, as occasionally happens in the St. Lawrence. There has been some discussion as to the length of time during which Hudson strait and bay might be navigated each year. There does not appear to be much evidence that the straits any more than the bay is closed at any season.
Why be faint-hearted in this matter, especially if we get a project in the manner described by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler), and if we approach it in that way with the idea of having a great family of Canadian provinces, each with some regard for the interests of the other, the strong provinces of the centre, if they find it necessary to impose something on the weaker provinces, compensating them in some way? I try to speak for the. western provinces when I say that we feel shut in there sometimes, like rats in a trap. We want to get out to the world by the short cut. Everybody in these days is always on the look-out for short cuts. In Ottawa, for instance, if a man can save half a step, he will cut across somebody's lot. That is what we want to do. but we want to do it legally
and practically. This means a great development for us. We never can do our best in the west until we get that port, or until we know it is either a port or a bad dream. We want to make a spoon or spoil a horn and we believe we can make a spoon. These are some of the reasons why we believe we can, and if we do, you will hear no more of this croaking, some of it justified, that has been going on. Those who have studied out these matters know things are not going aright. They know the heft of opinion and influence is down here and they feel put upon, irritated. They look to the west, with the mountains rising up to the heavens. They look to the east; they have never lived here and it is a long distance away. They are afraid of the east; they do not like the look of it, because they do not know us The story takes a great deal of telling when many others are telling the other side of it. We want to get out through that way and nobody will prosper more as a result of that than the east. In that way you will get the old settlers with their hearts aglow with new hope, and that is what brings the new settlers. When the old settlers feel that they are doing something, getting somewhere, becoming a factor in the country, they will go home and tell the new one3 to come out. They will say to them: This is a goodly land; we are well treated here; we have a good country and we are getting along nicely. You will not get new settlers in the right numbers until that happens, and when it happens Montreal will grow bigger and better than ever, so will Quebec, so will the Maritime provinces and all the east generally. Our purchasing capacity will be increased, and if you in the east make your prices reasonable, we shall buy Canadian goods in preference and not be doing as we did after reciprocity was defeated, when many of us, setting our teeth, said: Well, they cannot make us buy from them anyway. That is a bad spirit. I am glad to say we are getting ashamed of it and, wherever there is a disposition to make the duty reasonable, a duty for revenue, such as we have on agricultural implements now, the old spirit is coming back and we say: Other things being equal, we will buy Canadian goods. But after reciprocity was defeated, we did not have that spirit at all, far from it. I will not, however, go into that. Dr. Bell continues:
The only harbours on the west side of Hudson bay are those formed by the mouths of the rivers, but none of them, with the exception of Churchill harbour can be entered by vessels drawing more than ten or eleven feet and only at high water even by these.

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
A harbour such as that of Churchill on Hudson bay would have the advantage over Quebec or Montreal of communicating directly with the open sea, and hence in the autumn vessels would not be liable to be frozen in.
That is similar to testimony that I have read by another party, so I will not repeat it:
Churchill harbour does not freeze up until November and the sea is open close to it during the whole winter.
Salt water! Many people have the idea that this is a fresh-water bay. It is not; it is the Atlantic ocean. You can be in the middle of the strait and not see land on either side. You would not know that you were not in the Atlantic if you were there in the summer time. Of course, at other times of the year, you would be aware that you were not in the Atlantic. Many icebergs can be seen in the north Atlantic as late as August. Why should you bump into them more in Hudson bay than on the Atlantic? This talk about icebergs has been just an excuse. Captain Bernier, in another place, says that the Hudson bay is navigable for at least four months in the year, and with a ten per cent addition to the cost of the construction of our boats by adding a proper plating to withstand the ice pressure, you would have another month added, making five, if not six months that the bay is navigable. Another quotation:
Hudson Bay. The western shore is. low and affords but one well-sheltered spacious and perfectly safe harbour, Churchill, situated 200 miles from York factory.
Perfectly safe harbour! Would the mariner on the seven seas not sigh for a perfectly safe harbour when the storm from without threatens his vessel? Why do we not carry out this project? There is a story which I may as well tell now-I know the gentleman's name, but I will not mention it-that
9 p.m. somebody got a homestead on Churchill harbour, securing all the water front, and that he sold many town lots. Hon. members will remember the boom time and some of us here probably got stung, perhaps not as regards that place, but as regards others which had existence only on paper. This was one of the great ports of the world! Possibly somebody had been reading this and thought the development was going to take place right away. He did not know that there were as many, not mutinous, but faint-hearted officers on board as Columbus had, who wanted to turn back. I do not know what government was responsible in this connection and feel quite free to speak about it; but somebody said that Churchill was not tlhe port the man who homesteaded there thought it was, and some engineer advised them to go down to

Nelson, at least to get away from the ambitious homesteader and to open the port at Nelson. What about the engineer? The only explanation I ever heard was this and I can understand it. An engineer would not have much of a job opening up Churchill. The Lord himself made Churchill and you cannot improve on His handiwork, but no such provision was made at Nelson and an engineer had opportunities there. Why go to Churchill? You will never make a record at Churchill for any engineer because the work is all done. Here is Nelson, exposed to the sea, an uncertain channel, better, it is true, than we thought it was a few years ago. The season opens up a little earlier at Nelson, but there are low tides, great mud flats, with a channel away off from dry land, with half a mile of steel trestling to get to it, quite a considerable quantity of dump to get to the steel trestling, and an artificial island at the end of that. Imagine that! Just a row like these desks for half a mile of steel trestles to go across a mud flat to the channel which is constantly changing at Nelson. Then you have to build a great island on which to erect elevators like those at Montreal. The man who built on sand was, it seems to me, a wise man in comparison with this one. Why did they go there? There has been spent on that harbour up to date about six million dollars, and it is believed that Churchill could be established as a port for one-half of what it would take to complete the harbour at Nelson. Those of you who know what dredging means will realize how slow a government dredge can be, especially if you have ever gone down the St. Lawrence and looked, at some of .the locks there: the lock-keepers have to put up a picket to see whether the dredges are moving or not. As to dredging Nelson harbour, you would have to wait from now till the crack of doom to get results. Those gentlemen who are familiar with the Saskatchewan river no doubt know that the channel is seldom twice in the same place, for it is nothing but shifting sand; and those who are still more familiar with the bay of Fundy know what it is like there: the tide digs in here and digs in there and the least little thing will divert the course, so that you have it goring Into the opposite bank, sometimes beneficially to the land adjoining. The assumption is that the engineers in this instance, seeing an opportunity of doing something by which they couild become famous, by making the impossible possible, decided upon Nelson. But as Captain Bernier says, Canada is too poor to carry out. a stunt of that kind just now. Shall we therefore, in the face of these

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
evidences, persist in following what is apparently a hopeless course? Possibly I was waylaid by designing men when I was out there, but I met different classes of people from some of whom I gathered that the opinion was that. Nelson was not regarded as satisfactory. I met some engineers who I am sure would not give me wrong information, but I will not give their names inasmuch as it might get them into trouble. They are men of high repute whose word I would take and they declared that a mistake had been made, although they did not want to talk much about it. But there was no doubt as to the opinion held by more talkative people such as trappers, miners and fishermen. Let me quote from Lieut. A. R. Gordon, of the government expedition of 1SS6:
This (Churchill) harbour is admirably suited for a railway terminus. The necessary docks could be easily and cheaply built, and the deep water basin enlarged at small cost. Stone is lying at the water's edge ready to be laid into docks and piers and Nature seems to have left little to be done in order to make this a capacious port fit for doing a business of great magnitude."
There is no equivocation at all about that. Then why do we go to the other place? I do not know', and the explanation that is offered, is not sound. The explanation, about shifting to Nelson to get ahead of that ambitious homesteader who squatted at Churchill, will not do. Can anyone imagine engineers arguing that they would risk their reputation by doing something that might prove a failure merely in the hope that that reputation would be enhanced if the undertaking were successful, when the chances of success were so very small? Can anyone imagine such a thing? That explanation I cannot understand. Human nature, Mr. Speaker, is so strangely contradictory that if Churchill had been decided upon some people would have advocated Nelson. But there is no doubt about the fact that the great majority of those who know anything about this matter are agreed that the evidences in favour of Churchill are incontrovertible; there is a great value there that we have overlooked.
One of the advantages about Nelson is that it is open ten days earlier owing to the fact that it is further south by 120 miles. But the deciding factor is not the earlier opening of Nelson harbour; the important thing is the navigation of the Hudson strait. So that the fact of Nelson being open ten days earlier is immaterial. On the other hand it is 90 miles nearer to tide-water to go by Nelson, that is to say, to go via Churchill a distance of 90 miles further by rail haul. The only compensating factor would be that much less of
a water haul, which is not nearly so important as 90 miles by land. In addition to that there is from Churchill to Kettle rapids on this side a certain amount of muskeg. But there is no danger in that, because the muskeg is easily removed; you can roll it off like a carpet and let it freeze. There is no great engineering difficulty involved in it, and for that matter three of us could attend to it ourselves. It would not be true to say that it is not cold up there, because you do feel the cold; but it is sheltered and no wind breaks are required nor is there any need of snow fences. And it is some 400 miles with a drop of S00 feet towards the bay. It is the only road in North America that has not a bonded debt and there are no dangerous level crossings. I will quote from Captain S. W. Bartlett, in the Cruise of the Neptune, 1903-4:
The mouths of all the large rivers to the southward of Churchill are more or less blocked by deposits of sand and clay brought down by the streams. In consequence of these obstructions only small craft can enter the harbours inside the mouths of these rivers, and larger ships are obliged to lay in the dangerous roadsteads usually several miles away from the nearest dry land.
The approach to the harbour of Churchill, if aided by a few beacon lights, would be comparatively safe, ic the channel of approach is fairly deep and wide. Once outside the points of the mouth, the harbour extends up stream about a mile and has an average width of half a mile, with a couple of shallow places in the upper part that might easily be removed by dredging: the general depth of the harbour being from four to four and one-half fathoms.
Now I am a believer in the Hudson bay route and I take some satisfaction after all in the thought that it has not been rushed on to Nelson, for if these statements are true it would have been a calamity to do that and would have meant the ruin of the whole project for the present generation. It is true that one generation has worn itself away in anticipation of the achievement of this great enterprise, but it would have worn another generation away waiting to get real practical developments via Nelson. That is my opinion and I have given my authorities. And there is no one authority amongst them that so convinces me as the evidence of Captain Bernier. I do not by any means despise our scientific men; indeed, I have a profound respect for men of science, men of engineering knowledge and skill; I think very highly of our experts. We could not possibly do without the experts and I respect them. But in this particular case I have still greater respect for a man like Captain Bernier who has been captain of vessels continuously from the age of seventeen. He knows what he is talking about, as only a man with actual experience can know. For these reasons I have some satisfaction in the

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
thought that the Nelson project has not been carried out. I want to see the road kept in shipshape as far as Kettle rapids, and I want to see the question settled for all time as to which port will be developed. It is not for me to go further on that point than I have gone; the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) will discuss this question among others in his annual statement on the railways. If we reach the resolution of the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Knox) the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) will probably have something to say with regard to it.
I came back from Hudson bay and went to Fort William for the purpose of coming east by the St. Lawrence route. There was great congestion at that time, about the beginning of September, the wheat was going up; there was no demand for it from the British market, and it was accumulating rapidly at Montreal1 and backing up to Port Colbome. We could not get a wheat boat to Port Colborne, so we had to take an ordinary passenger boat. When we got there we found six or seven large upper lake vessels with a capacity of from three to five hundred thousand bushels apiece, which were unable to discharge their cargoes into the elevators. Our eastern route has become obsolete; it is ten or fifteen years behind the requirements of the country. When we get the Welland canal1 completed, however, you will have the upper lake boats passing right through to Brockville or Kingston or Prescott, wherever the terminus may be, and they will be able to carry grain more cheaply than they are doing now under present conditions. You will also have the railway facilities with only one divisional point to cover and it will be possible to avoid congestion at Prescott or wherever the terminus is. We have only half the storage space in Montreal that is available at Buffalo. People are wondering why the Saskatchewan Co-operative elevator people are building an elevator at Buffalo, but it is because they have so much more space there. They have abandoned practically all these obsolete canals and are getting the grain through to New York fast enough to prevent congestion. If a vessel has to wait three weeks at Port Colbome before the cargo can be discharged, sometimes even before the crew can be discharged, freight can never be drawn cheaply. We cannot expect cheap transportation on our inland waters until the Welland canal is completed. Some of the larger boats may not be able to go through the canal, but most of them will. Those that cannot go through will discharge at Port Colbome, and those that can go 
through will proceed to the terminal point and
by that means nearly all the benefits of the deepened St. Lawrence can be secured without the large cost of additional improvements from Prescott to Montreal; because you have the Canadian National, you have the Canadian Pacific and the canal boats available to keep the grain moving. When we have more population to pay for it, the Welland canal project will one day be completed and I am satisfied that we Should get a reduction of two or three cents in the cost of the carrying of grain to Montreal. It costs four times as much per mile to haul grain from Port Colborne to Montreal as it does to haul it from Fort William to Port Colbome. It took us nineteen hours to go through the Welland canal, and we were stopped for two hours by fog. If that occurred on the Hudson bay you would have heard about it all over the country, but you do not hear about it when it is on the Welland canal. All honour, I say, to the men of a hundred years ago who started the canal system. Some of our grandparents came up the rapids from Montreal by any means they could employ- paddled, poled or walked; and I cannot pay too high a tribute to the Canadians of that day who conceived and carried out the canal systems on the St. Lawrence. But they are inadequate to meet the greater needs of the present day. It took sixty-eight hours to go from Port Colborne to Montreal, a distance of 320 miles, which is at the rate of 4i miles an hour. You cannot draw grain cheaply that way; it is only one and a half times faster than a relay of horses could do it. In the 64 miles of canal the rate was less than two miles an hour. Let us not look for cheap freight rates under these mediaeval conditions; they were fine in their time but they cannot meet the needs of to-day. It will take six years to finish the canal, and when it is completed I should say that three-quarters of the benefits of the deepened St. Lawrence system would not be any better than the facilities provided by the Welland canal when the upper lake boats can discharge at Prescott or the terminal point in that part of the St. Lawrence system.
We have discussed lake rates in this House, sometimes rather heatedly, and I had almost persuaded myself that the remedy was to remove the coastal laws. It sounds good; it is getting a crack at somebody. But when the conditions at Port Colborne, for instance, are such as I have described, six or seven big vessels finding it impossible to discharge cargo-and prices were not up at that time, because the carriers were under contract early in the season; some of the grain was being taken to Montreal at six cents a bushel-[DOT]

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
would not the removal of the coastal laws and the operation of twice as many boats simply make the congestion worse? Unless you have actually seen the condition it is hard to grasp its significance, but let me illustrate it in this way: An elevator is receiving grain very rapidly; ten wagons are waiting to unload. Would it cure the situation to bring on ten more, or would it not make the congestion worse? Do not misunderstand me: at a time when there is no congestion at Montreal or Port Colborne and cargoes can be discharged with despatch, then if there is imposition, if there are excessive rates as there were two years ago, the admission of more tonnage would provide a measure of competition and possibly afford some relief. But only under those conditions should it be done.
It seems to me there is no justification for the upper lake boats charging more to haul grain to the bay ports or Port Colborne than is being charged to take it to Buffalo, just a little bit further. It is only when there is congestion that 'there is any justification for high charges. Consequently, when there is no congestion, the control that is provided for in the act should be exercised in some way to see that advantage is not taken and the freight rates put up and more charged for the shorter distance than for the long haul. I can imagine Port McNicoll and other ports being in the very same position that Port Colborne was, and not being able to unload, because a lot of. our grain goes from these bay ports to Montreal. The year before last 26,000.000 bushels went by rail, and if there was congestion at the bay elevators the boats iwould have the same difficulty, idling around there for several days, not being able to get rid of their cargo, and not being able to haul as cheaply as if the grain went right through to Buffalo. You cannot have a crew doing nothing and getting their board and pay, and draw grain cheaply. So I have come to the conclusion that what we need is more storage at Montreal, quick despatch at Port Colborne, the Welland canal finished at least as far as Prescott, and then we will have cheap rates on our inland waters. In the meantime we have had some control. I do not want to go into any of the controversial phases of that question, but the fact that we have had no complaints for the last two years is the best evidence that there is not the situation to-day that there was two years ago, and it is 'attributable 'to our legislation and our control, and to the possible further use of that control. Two years ago, was not every newspaper in the west
and every Progressive member in this House from the west shouting from the housetops of the exactions on the lakes? You have restored the Crowsnest rates, they said, but what you gave with one hand you took away with the other by these lake rates. You could not get that out of their heads, because they knew the pinch was there. Do you mean to say there is a pinch now, and1 that somebody has come along with an anaesthetic so that they do not feel the pinch? Can you find one newspaper in the west complaining about rates on the lakes to-day? So, Mr. Speaker, I say that if we can give as satisfactory control on the ocean as we are getting to-day on the inland waters of Canada, and with as little discontent on the ocean as we have to-day on the lakes, we will certainly have done a great work. I say, Mr. Speaker, that there cannot foe exactions such as we heard described two years ago when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low) was putting through his bill, there cannot be these exactions and alleged losses by the farmers without them knowing it; and if they do know it, they have certainly been wonderfully quiet about it. No, Mr. Speaker, conditions are not the same to-day. We have not had occasion to use all the power we took in that bill. I admit frankly there were phases of that legislation that were not workable in the beginning, but where is the bill that has not some weakness in it? For two months it was unworkable; for two months the rates were admittedly higher while the negotiations were going on, but as soon as that was ironed out the whole matter was adjusted, and has stayed adjusted! until this day. Will anybody tell me where there is a legislative body in the world to-day that can frame legislation which it never needs to change? I will admit we made mistakes, but we corrected the weaknesses, and we met the situation, and that is what we are going to do on the Atlantic and on the Pacific.

speechtext:
Even doctors will
disagree; engineers also will disagree. I remember hearing a report at an annual meeting of engineers east of here; they had the most hilarious time in the world over it. I pin my faith, in what I said, on practical men who are doing things every day, and I have found such men to be reliable all through life, both on land and on water. I am quite aware of what will be said on the prairies. I know it will be said that I am trying to raise some objection to this project going forward. I know that. I have been long enough in public life to know the danger spots, but I am going to take a chance because I feel in my heart that I am right.
Now, I do not want to keep my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition any longer
in a condition of suspense about the Maritime situation. All our opinions regarding these rate matters-those of us especially who do not live in the Maritimes-have to be given with some qualifications. I never visited the Maritimes but once in my life, and that was a year ago last summer. I spent three and a half weeks there, and I was certainly charmed with that country. I heard the grievances of the people at first hand, and they put me in mind very much of our own grievances in the west. As a result, my heart went out to the Maritime provinces. People who suffer similar adversity will be drawn together; adversity always draws men together better than prosperity-a common difficulty, a common danger, if you like, common troubles. I tried to analyze their difficulties to see if, in my own department, I could contribute anything towards alleviating those troubles; and do you know, Mr. Speaker, that after searching fore and aft, after searching all over the country and looking into rate troubles for a possible solution, I found that those troubles were not as numerous as we were told.
Now the freight question was a great difficulty; it has existed for years in connection with the mines. I am not a miner at all, but with my companions I went down into the Glace Bay mines. In fact, I visited the whole mining area there. I talked to the miners, I was in their homes, and I ate with them. As I say, I went down in the Glace Bay shaft for 900 feet where the mine goes under Sydhey harbour, and I wondered to myself how much farther they were going to burrow there before they would, for economic reasons, have to quit? It was all very new and very wonderful to me. I noticed also that many of the miners lived in better houses, notwithstanding all that has been said, than I had lived in for twenty years. I saw beautiful shower baths there; you did not meet with many of those on the prairies in the first twenty years of its history. There was hardship, there always is hardship; the miners had a great many idle days, and there were a great many difficulties to be overcome. There is bound to be distress. There is distress there now, but I am not going to enter into that side of the question. What I want to point out is that the difficulties that could be remedied were few in number. The coal situation seemed to be one of them. The freight situation seemed to be another; the building up of the ports in the Maritime provinces seemed to be another. I could not help feeling that there was another difficulty there that nobody has said much about, and that is

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
the difficulty of getting a market for the potatoes of the Maritime provinces, not so grievous a situation at the time I speak of as it is now. The potato question was a difficult one for many years, but this year it was largely overcome by the system of certifying to the potatoes, which certification was so valuable that those products entered the United States, in spite of the duty, and good money was realized by the shippers. The difficulty in regard to the Maritime province ports was solved two years ago by the Minister of Finance through the medium of the preferential tariff. I am right in saying that difficulty is solved because now over 99 per cent of dutiable goods coming to Canada enter by our own ports. These are two difficulties out of the four that have been removed.
What is going to be done with regard to the mining difficulty? We have discussed the mining situation in this House every year since I came 'here. Two difficulties out of three have been solved, but the most acute one still exists. The Minister of the Interior has announced once or twice this session his plan with regard to the coking of bituminous coal from the Maritime provinces. Last year he announced a plan of subventions to permit of the transportation of Canadian coal much farther into the interior, and as a result of the increased demand to enable the miners to produce that much more coal. What more could we do? We could not keep on giving subventions. The Premier of Nova Scotia came up here at the head of a large delegation and interviewed the government. One of the most pressing requests he made was that the duty should be increased on slack coal. He pointed out that a great deal of fraud was being committed and I found out later that his argument in this connection was well founded. He charged that slack coal was being imported under the fourteen cent rate of duty and being mixed with run-of-mine under the 53 cent rate. He, therefore, asked that the duty on slack coal be raised to encourage the mining of that fuel. The Premier of Nova Scotia, accompanied as he was by a number of representatives of Cape Breton, presented a petition to the government on the question asking for that and other things. There was a very large delegation that entirely filled the railway committee room. They found that two or three of their grievances had been remedied before they had time to ask for their solution. However, the coal difficulty still remains. I do not take the ground that a national solution should always have to be discovered for a local difficulty, not at all.

We were in the midst of working out some of the Maritime difficulties capable of solution when the present strike, or lockout, or whatever you choose to call it, occurred in these mines. The Besco people in the first place took the ground that they could not afford to pay the wages then prevailing. They had cut down the days of labour. There was not enough profit in it to be able to pay the wages the miners wanted, they got at loggerheads, and the whole thing was shut down, to the loss of all. What were we to do? The local authorities began to solve the distress question at the other end, and while this budget is a Canadian budget, it is essentially one designed to assist the Maritime provinces, not only in regard to coal but in regard to fishing industries and such like. We have adopted the policy of dropping the item of slack coal and lowering the duty on run-of-mine coal three cents; and otherwise we adjust the tariff, put it up on slack coal if you like, which represents about three million tons, and put it down on run-of-mine which represents about eleven million tons. Already in this House the hon. member for Kent, New Brunswick (Mr. Doucet) has reprimanded us for reducing the duty on run-of-mine coal. We have reduced the duty on run-of-mine coal and run up the duty on slack coal, removed it altogether from the tariff schedule, and put a straight fifty cents on the run-of-mine coal. Someone asks on what percentage would that be on the slack coal? There is no percentage in it. I do not know the price of coal, but it is not levied on the price. Hon. members can soon figure it out. It is a comparatively easy matter. It is a duty of fifty cents per ton. That is done with a two or threefold purpose. One is to encourage the Maritime province miners in the desire to reach further out into the markets of Ontario and Quebec. That was the original conception of confederation; and after violating the spirit of that contract at confederation, by taking away from them those special freight rates that they had all those years, and putting them into the consolidated system, then, if you are going to carry out the policy I have mentioned, of taking care of the smaller provinces, you must do something to compensate them for the thing that they had at confederation and which they lost.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Have we restored
to the people down there the same ad valorem duty that they had when the fourteen cent rate was put in? By reason of the increase in the value of the commodity that fourteen cent rate was getting less and less on an ad valorem basis. Perhaps I should have gone into it to find out the exact price on which that was levied. I do not know my self to-day whether we are getting more duty. I question very much if we are giving more protection than we were giving when it was fourteen cents when we had seventy cent coal. We have restored what was slipping away from us year by year as a result of the increased value of slack coal. Was that such a whale of a lot to do for them? I am one of those who believes that that is going to bring some redress. If the mines down there can be made more profitable it should benefit the labourer. I have hired too much labour in my time to be told that when an institution is profitable some of that profit will not go to the labourer. I know it will go to the labourer. I have hired labour all my life,
and when I make money some more of it goes to my labourers. When I do not make money I have to make a hard bargain with my labourers if I am going to carry on. Everybody who employs labour knows that.. I do not care who the Besco people are, I would not care if they were twice the steel corporation they claim to be, in their self interest they will keep their mines going if it is humanly possible, and if they are able to secure something better than they have had, if this is increased protection, and if they are enabled to carry on and make more money, part of it will go to the miners, and they will get to work and the trouble will be at an end. I am not accustomed to people going on strike. I am accustomed when a man will not work foi me to have him quit and go somewhere else But that is not the way of organized labour. Now how are you going to improve things for the Besco people or for the miners? I have talked with a lot of miners who are not in favour of the strike. I have been in the mines and know some people there, and I know there is great distress there while they are on strike. Human nature is the same thing the world over. The local authorities are working with us from their own standpoint, and incidentally we are helping them from our standpoint. I would ask the Progressives, particularly those from the west who have been working in co-operation to some extent with the Maritime and eastern provinces during the last two or three years, especially the Maritimes, when the Crowsnest pass question was up, who were standing by the western men back on the prairies stronger than the Maritime province men or stronger than the Island men, and again when we were trying to work out the compulsory wheat board clause after the war was over? They said let the west have it if it is going to do them any good. Last year when nearly all the changes were favourable to the western men did anyone see any one of the Maritime men gag at it? Those from Ontario did some squirming about. They stood up for their rights. But one hon, member stood out- too strongly, the gentleman from St. Antoine, he resigned and he was sorry afterwards. But it shows that we went as far as we could, as far as public sentiment would allow. In fact, we went so far that even one of the Progressive group voted with the Tories. The Maritime men stood to a man behind the west.
Long before I had the honour of coming to this House, I often wondered what evil

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
genius possessed the people of the three prairie provinces and of the three Maritime provinces, whose interests as regards the tariff and many other things are almost identical. I question if there are in this House sounder and more practical men on the tariff than those from the Maritime provinces. Why do we not have some more fellowship and understanding with each other when we have so many interests in common? The same is true of rural Quebec. Indeed, as a matter of fact, you might say that it is practically true now of almost all Quebec and I hope that will continue to be the case. Here is an oportunity for the men on the prairies to reciprocate. They say that they are in favour of reciprocity, but let them not say that they are in favour of it only if it is all their own way. When something is to be done for the Maritimes, let them have their protection. When protection ceases to be in existence in the Dominion of Canada, then they may cast a stone at this in the Maritimes. I do not know whether protection in Canada will ever cease or not; but if the west refuses to accept this budget on the ground of what is claimed to be high protection on coal, but which was agreed to by Premier Greenfield and many others in the west and as regards which the only kick came from protected Ontario, I am afraid our western friends are losing an opportunity of showing a reciprocal feeling for the Maritimes, for what the Maritimes have been prepared to do for the west at every opportunity since we have come down here. Is that a right attitude to cultivate as regards the Maritimes? Should men with common interests not work together in unison? When the delegation from the west went down to the Maritimes, as I read their after dinner speeches and learned of the good times they had, I understand their hearts went out to the Maritimes Did you see, Mr. Speaker, the accounts in regard to the delegation from the Maritime provinces that went to the west? Certain newspaper representatives from the Maritimes went through the western country. All our leading journals held out the right hand to them and were willing to solve their problems in any way humanly possible, because we felt that they were suffering under adverse conditions and we were willing to help them. Personally, I have been here long enough to know that we are all going to vote on this budget to suit our own interests We are all keeping an eye on the folks back home. Sometimes we do not do so but we should. There is another broader vision even than that. Are we going to shirk this first oppor-unity of working out in harmony with the 
eastern provinces, an incidental solution of this difficulty in Glace Bay, or are we going to refuse to reciprocate? I leave that there, feeling assured that possibly the difficulties may be solved. I understand my hon. friends' difficulties. We have all been born and bred, I was going to say, to hate protection, and it is hard to get over our early training. But as long as it is here-and it is here-some of these distressed places are surely justified in saying: Give us a little of what seems good for us, particularly when it saddles itself on to the protected industries of Ontario, and, if you like, Quebec. Is that a satisfactory answer to my hon. friend? Have I been candid enough?
